meta.title: SkyWater Technology — Thomas Sonderman's DoD Trusted Foundry through CHIPS Act, Florida Center of Neovation, and specialty process scaling
meta.abstract: SkyWater Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: SKYT) is a Bloomington, Minnesota-headquartered US-domiciled specialty semiconductor foundry — the only US-owned pure-play foundry serving the DoD Trusted Foundry program. The company emerged from a 2017 spin-out of the Cypress Semiconductor Bloomington fab and listed on NASDAQ via IPO in April 2021. SkyWater operates specialty derivative process technologies (RF SOI, MEMS, mixed-signal, superconducting electronics, photonics, advanced packaging) for defense, aerospace, government, and commercial customers. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 has centered on (a) CHIPS Act support and Florida Center of Neovation (CoN) capacity expansion, (b) DoD Trusted Foundry production for defense primes (Northrop Grumman, RTX, Lockheed Martin-affiliated programs), (c) capacity utilization scaling at the Bloomington fab, and (d) the broader US-domestic-foundry resurgence under industrial policy.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The US Foundry Imperative

SkyWater Technology occupies a narrow but strategically vital position in the global semiconductor landscape: the only publicly listed, US-owned pure-play specialty foundry operating exclusively on domestic soil, with a Department of Defense Trusted Foundry designation that few competitors can replicate. Through 2024 and 2025, that positioning translated into structural demand from defence primes, government research programmes, and a burgeoning quantum computing sector that required fabrication it could trust and locate within American borders.

Trading on Nasdaq as SKYT, the company operates from its primary 200-millimetre fabrication facility in Bloomington, Minnesota — a site with more than four decades of semiconductor heritage — ~~and from the Florida Center of Neovation, an advanced packaging facility leased from Osceola County in Kissimmee, Florida.~~ ==from the Florida Center of Neovation, an advanced packaging facility leased from Osceola County in Kissimmee, Florida, and from SkyWater Texas, the 200-millimetre Fab 25 in Austin, Texas acquired from Infineon Technologies in June 2025 and reported as a distinct facility and operating segment.== Thomas Sonderman has served as President and Chief Executive since the 2017 spin-out, when private-equity firm Oxbow Industries acquired the Bloomington fab from Cypress Semiconductor and rebranded it SkyWater Technology. The company listed on Nasdaq in April 2021 and has operated as a capital-intensive, operating-loss business through its capacity-building phase, using a combination of post-IPO equity, customer-funded capital expenditure, and government grants to finance expansion.

## Two Revenue Lines, One Conversion Cycle

SkyWater's commercial model runs on two reported revenue streams: Advanced Technology Services (ATS), covering custom process development funded by customers or government programmes, typically through multi-year engineering agreements; and Wafer Services, which captures production-volume revenue once a developed process moves into manufacturing. The central investment variable is the reliability and pace with which ATS engagements convert into Wafer Services volumes — a cycle the company characterises as spanning 18 to 36 months.

For fiscal 2025 — the twelve months ended 28 December 2025 — legacy SkyWater ATS development revenue reached $212.5 million, with Wafer Services contributing $25.2 million from Bloomington. Legacy revenue in aggregate fell approximately 22 per cent year-over-year, reflecting federal budget delays that compressed government-funded ATS bookings across the first half. Sonderman had flagged the structural risk plainly in May 2025: "We are confident in our ability to execute towards another record ATS revenue year in 2025, provided that the funding delays in Washington, DC are resolved soon."

The consolidated headline number — total revenue of $442.1 million, up 29 per cent year-on-year — was driven by a transformative inorganic step. In June 2025, SkyWater completed the acquisition of Infineon Technologies' 200-millimetre Fab 25 in Austin, Texas, for approximately $93 million in cash and working capital, financed through a new $350 million revolving credit facility. The acquired facility contributed $175.6 million in Wafer Services revenue across roughly six months of consolidated reporting, immediately exceeding management's early projections. At full run-rate, Fab 25 was expected to add more than $300 million annually and approximately 400,000 wafer starts per year. The group delivered adjusted EBITDA of $53.2 million (12.0 per cent margin) and a narrow operating loss of $2.6 million — the closest SkyWater had come to operating breakeven since its April 2021 IPO. ([SkyWater IR, FY2025 results](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2026/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx))

## ~~Florida and the CHIPS Act Architecture~~ ==Florida DoD Awards and the Bloomington CHIPS PMT==

The Florida Center of Neovation carried two principal government funding streams. In December 2024, SkyWater and Deca Technologies announced a five-year DoD contract awarded through Osceola County worth $120 million — with options extending to $190 million — to establish domestic fan-out wafer-level packaging capabilities, a class of advanced packaging that accounted for less than three per cent of US domestic production. "This agreement with the county enables SkyWater Florida to execute all aspects of the initial DOD award of up to $120 million and stand up our fan-out wafer level packaging capabilities by utilizing Deca's industry leading technology," Sonderman said at the time. ([SkyWater press release](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-florida-and-deca-technologies-announce-120m-dod-award-to-expand-advanced-packaging-capabilities-in-osceola-county-florida/))

Separately, through the Florida Semiconductor Coalition, the company accessed $36.5 million in Department of Commerce funding ==— an EDA-administered grant rather than a direct CHIPS Act award —== for cleanroom expansion and tooling installation at the CoN. ([SkyWater press release](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-to-leverage-36-5m-department-of-commerce-grant-to-the-florida-semiconductor-coalition-to-expand-its-advanced-packaging-facility-operations-in-florida/)) ==The sole public CHIPS for America preliminary memorandum of terms negotiated by SkyWater was for Bloomington, not Florida.== The Bloomington fab received its own commitment: a preliminary CHIPS for America memorandum of terms for up to $16 million in direct federal funding, supplemented by $19 million from Minnesota's Forward Fund, targeting a 30 per cent increase in production capacity at the 90-nanometre and 130-nanometre nodes and approximately 70 new positions. ([NIST announcement, December 2024](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/12/biden-harris-administration-announce-preliminary-terms-coherent-skywater)) CoN advanced-packaging facilitisation progressed ahead of plan through the fourth quarter of 2025, though tooling installation cost overruns of approximately $9.3 million — attributed to inflation-related pricing — trimmed gross margins. Tool installations were scheduled for completion in early 2026, with prototype customer builds targeted for later that year.

## Quantum, DoD, and the Open Questions

SkyWater's DARPA-funded superconducting electronics programme became a commercial growth vector as quantum hardware development accelerated. The company closed 2025 with eight commercial ATS quantum engagements — four signed in the third quarter alone — with quantum ATS revenues rising more than 30 per cent across the full year. "We believe our exclusively U.S. focus and Trusted status as a pure-play foundry partner make us the ideal manufacturing partner," Sonderman said following the record third quarter. ([SkyWater IR, Q3 2025](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Record-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx))

The dossier's analytical questions frame as follows. The ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion cycle — still the primary revenue-predictive variable — requires ATS engagements in Bloomington and at the CoN to move into production at sufficient scale and pace against a lag structure measured in years. Florida ramp execution must absorb a $120 million DoD programme delivery obligation alongside CHIPS Act milestone conditions and an aggressive facilitisation timeline, without further cost creep. Competitive positioning holds against GlobalFoundries' overlapping Trusted Foundry certifications, TSMC's advancing Arizona presence at finer nodes, and X-Fab's specialty analogue and mixed-signal processes — each competing for a distinct but partially overlapping customer set. In January 2026, IonQ announced a $1.8 billion agreement to acquire SkyWater at $35.00 per share — framing the combination as the world's only vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform — ~~with shareholders approving the transaction and close expected in the second or third quarter of 2026~~ ==with SkyWater stockholders having approved the transaction on May 8, 2026 and the deal accordingly no longer subject to a shareholder vote at the May 23, 2026 snapshot, leaving only remaining regulatory closing conditions ahead of an expected close in the second or third quarter of 2026==, a deal that would embed SkyWater's Trusted Foundry infrastructure into the quantum-computing stack with Sonderman remaining in the chief executive role. ([IonQ announcement](https://investors.ionq.com/news/news-details/2026/IonQ-to-Acquire-SkyWater-Technology-Creating-the-Only-Vertically-Integrated-Full-Stack-Quantum-Platform-Company/default.aspx))

chapters.title: From 2017 Cypress Bloomington spin-out through 2021 NASDAQ IPO to CHIPS Act scaling
chapters.body:
## Roots in Copper-Lined Walls: Control Data to Cypress

The semiconductor facility that became SkyWater Technology was born not in Silicon Valley but on the Minnesota prairie, a product of the Cold War's demand for secure electronics. Control Data Corporation, the Minneapolis supercomputer pioneer, operated chip-making operations at a Bloomington site whose concrete walls were lined with copper sheeting to defeat electronic eavesdropping — a physical imprint of the building's intended purpose that would prove prescient decades later. When Control Data sold its chip division in 1982 to investors who formed VTC Inc., and later reacquired and then divested it again, the facility passed through several hands before Cypress Semiconductor acquired it at the end of 1990 for approximately $14.7 million.

Cypress designated the site Fab 4 and invested heavily. In 1995 the company upgraded it to a 200mm wafer line — the first 200mm facility in the Cypress network — producing SRAM products, CMOS image sensors, and mixed-signal circuits including early Programmable System-on-Chip devices. Technology nodes eventually spanned 350nm through 90nm. Fab 4 also achieved Category 1A Trusted Foundry accreditation from the Defense Microelectronics Activity in 2010 under the entity name Cypress Minnesota Inc., cementing the site's role as a cleared supplier to the U.S. Department of Defense.

By the mid-2010s, Cypress was executing a manufacturing consolidation intended to improve gross margins, shifting volume toward its Fab 25 in Austin, Texas. ATREG Inc., a semiconductor asset advisory firm, was retained to market Fab 4. Cypress was acquired by Infineon Technologies in 2020, but by then the Bloomington sale had already been concluded.

## The Oxbow Transaction and a New Identity

On March 2, 2017, Cypress announced the sale of its Minnesota fab to Oxbow Industries, LLC for $30 million. The deal closed within weeks. Oxbow, headquartered in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, is a private equity and holding company managed by Loren A. Unterseher — a former M&A partner at Stinson Leonard Street LLP and investment banking veteran with stints at RBC/Dain Rauscher, Lazard Middle Market, and Craig-Hallum Capital Group, credited with completing over $2.5 billion in corporate finance transactions. The transaction transferred the capital stock of Cypress Minnesota Inc. rather than simply its assets, preserving the entity's operating history and, crucially, its existing regulatory accreditations.

The company launched on March 27, 2017 under the name **SkyWater Technology Foundry**, with a multi-year wafer supply agreement ensuring that Cypress — now transitioning toward Infineon's ownership — would remain an anchor customer. At founding, roughly 97 percent of revenue originated from that supply relationship, a concentration that would define the company's early commercial challenge. The site's DMEA Category 1A accreditation was re-certified in the new entity's name just nineteen days after closing, on March 20, 2017 — a priority that reflected management's understanding of where durable competitive advantage lay.

Thomas Sonderman arrived as President and Chief Executive approximately five months after the founding close, bringing eleven years at GlobalFoundries, where he had served as Vice President of Manufacturing Technology and was a key contributor to the 2009 spin-out of AMD's fabrication assets. His CV also included roles at AMD and Rudolph Technologies (now ONTO Innovation), and he held more than fifty patents. Sonderman defined the company's ambition in terms that blended commercial positioning with explicit national-interest framing: "Foundries were only offering standard processes and customers had to differentiate on design alone," he said in a later interview. "SkyWater uniquely had the ability to differentiate with process and design in a cohesive fashion." He described the broader mission as a "catalyst to restore domestic capability, secure trusted production, and reignite the spirit of innovation that defines this country" — language calibrated to an era of mounting concern about semiconductor supply-chain sovereignty.

## Diversification and the Path to NASDAQ

The four years between founding and public listing were a period of deliberate customer diversification and DoD program accumulation. Revenue concentration from the Cypress/Infineon supply agreement fell from approximately 97 percent at founding to roughly 60 percent by 2018, as SkyWater added four new wafer customers and expanded its Advanced Technology Services pipeline with defense and research agencies including DARPA and IARPA. A pivotal DoD contract arrived in October 2019, when the Department of Defense committed up to $170 million — with $80 million initially funded — to develop a radiation-hardened 90nm process (RH90) and expand cleanroom capacity by up to 15,000 square feet. The program involved technology transfer from MIT Lincoln Laboratory and positioned Bloomington as a strategically irreplaceable node in the defense electronics supply chain.

By the time SkyWater filed its S-1 registration statement on March 22, 2021, the former Cypress Semiconductor IDM fab had recast itself as the United States' only domestically owned and operated pure-play specialty semiconductor foundry — a designation that carried particular weight in the year following a global chip shortage and pandemic-era recognition of supply-chain fragility.

## The April 2021 IPO: $112 Million on NASDAQ

The IPO was priced on April 20, 2021, at **$14.00 per share** — the top of the indicated range, reflecting an upsized offering. Jefferies LLC and Cowen served as joint lead book-running managers, with Piper Sandler & Co. as book-running manager. SkyWater offered 6,960,000 primary shares; underwriters exercised their 30-day over-allotment option in full, adding 1,044,000 shares for a total of 8,004,000 shares sold. **Gross proceeds reached $112,056,000.** Net proceeds, after underwriting discounts and offering costs, totalled approximately $100.3 million. The company began trading on the NASDAQ Capital Market under the ticker **SKYT** on April 21, 2021.

At $14 per share and with ~~approximately 57 million shares outstanding~~ ==39,059,743 shares outstanding after full exercise of the over-allotment== — ~~Oxbow's Unterseher retained roughly 34 percent~~ ==Oxbow and affiliates retained approximately 71.7 percent== beneficial ownership post-listing — the offering implied a market capitalisation of approximately ~~$800 million~~ ==$547 million==. Proceeds were directed to working capital and general corporate purposes, explicitly including capital expenditures to fund growth. By the time of the prospectus, customer concentration had fallen further: Cypress/Infineon represented approximately 29 percent of revenue, and the DoD program and specialty-process customer base had materially broadened.

## Center of NeoVation: Osceola County and Advanced Packaging

Even as the Bloomington IPO was being prepared, SkyWater was quietly assembling its second act. The Center for NeoVation in Kissimmee, Florida — a 109,000-square-foot semiconductor facility in NeoCity, Osceola County, adjacent to the University of Central Florida — had been built as a state-backed microelectronics hub operated by a nonprofit entity called BRIDG. When UCF terminated its management agreement in 2019–2020 following state budget cuts, the facility was left without an operator, its 36,000 square feet of Class 1,000 and Class 10,000 cleanroom space and its six-million-pound vibration-dampening waffle slab foundation sitting largely idle.

Osceola County entered negotiations with SkyWater in late 2020. On January 25, 2021 — three months before the NASDAQ IPO — SkyWater signed a lease extending to **October 2044**, assuming UCF's position. The company committed to creating 220 jobs within five years and agreed to operate and maintain the center at no additional cost to the county. A $15 million termination fee would be payable to the county if SkyWater exited and no replacement operator was found within an 18-month notice period.

The strategic rationale was advanced packaging — the discipline of integrating multiple chiplets, dies, and components into a single system-in-package — an area almost entirely absent from U.S. domestic capability at that time. In September 2022, the facility attracted a $36.5 million grant from the U.S. Economic Development Administration's Build Back Better Regional Challenge, part of a $50.8 million award to the Florida Semiconductor Coalition led by Osceola County and including UCF, Valencia College, IMEC, Tokyo Electron, and SUSS MicroTec. SkyWater provided the required 20 percent match.

## CHIPS Act Era: RESHAPE and the Federal Bet

The most consequential inflection arrived on January 10, 2024, when SkyWater Florida and Deca Technologies announced a **$120 million Department of Defense contract** — with up to $70 million in additional options, totalling $190 million — to build fan-out wafer-level packaging capacity at the Kissimmee facility under the RESHAPE program. Deca's M-Series architecture and Adaptive Patterning technology would enable high-density multi-chip integration for defense primes. Five months later, on May 14, 2024, SkyWater Florida achieved its own DMEA Category 1A Trusted Supplier accreditation, completing a transition begun in 2017: 100 percent of the company's operational footprint was now DoD-trusted.

> "With very little advanced packaging taking place in the U.S., this poses national security and economic risks," Sonderman said at the May 2024 accreditation. "By reshoring this critical step, we can assure the integrity, quality and confidentiality of the design and manufacturing of microelectronics systems."

On December 6, 2024, the Biden-Harris Administration's CHIPS Program Office at the Department of Commerce announced preliminary terms of a direct-funding agreement with SkyWater of **up to $16 million** in federal CHIPS Act support for the Bloomington facility, paired with $19 million from Minnesota's Forward Fund state co-investment programme and the 25 percent Advanced Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit under IRS Section 48D. The programme targets a roughly 30 percent increase in 90nm and 130nm wafer production capacity and approximately 70 new Bloomington jobs. SkyWater projected over $350 million in combined investment across "this decade," with approximately $320 million expected in customer-funded capital expenditures through 2026.

> "We are pleased to receive this important proposed CHIPS funding," Sonderman said in December 2024. "We have been working to meet the specific needs of the Defense Industrial Base and commercial companies."

From a copper-shielded Cold War bunker acquired for $14.7 million, through a $30 million private-equity spin-out and a $112 million public market debut, to a nine-figure DoD packaging programme and a federal CHIPS imprimatur, the arc of the Bloomington fab and its Florida annex encapsulates Washington's belated wager on American semiconductor sovereignty.

chapters.title: ATS, Wafer Services, and the two-fab footprint
chapters.body:
## Two businesses inside one foundry

SkyWater Technology has never been a simple volume manufacturer. From its 2017 birth as an Oxbow Industries spin-out of the Cypress Semiconductor Bloomington fab through its April 2021 NASDAQ listing and into the CHIPS Act-supported expansion of the 2024–2026 period, the company has organised itself around two discrete but sequentially linked revenue streams: **Advanced Technology Services** (ATS) and **Wafer Services**. Understanding how one feeds the other — and on what timeline — is the essential key to reading SkyWater's financial history and its forward trajectory.

ATS encompasses custom process development: the engineering-service contracts under which SkyWater's technologists work alongside a customer to define, iterate, and qualify a novel semiconductor process. Wafer Services is the downstream consequence — volume production on the processes that survive qualification. The two segments sit at opposite ends of the same pipeline. ATS is lumpy and programme-driven; Wafer Services is steadier and capacity-constrained. The lag between a programme win in ATS and first volume revenue in Wafer Services has typically run eighteen to thirty-six months, a structural feature that makes SkyWater's near-term income statement a lagging indicator of its medium-term commercial position.

## Advanced Technology Services: engineering as the revenue anchor

ATS has historically been the larger of the two segments by revenue, a fact that reflects both SkyWater's strategic positioning and the economics of the US specialty foundry market. Defence agencies, research laboratories, and commercial customers with genuinely novel process requirements do not arrive at a foundry with a completed process specification; they arrive with a problem — a device concept, a system requirement, a frequency range, a power envelope — and they need a partner who can translate that requirement into manufacturable silicon. SkyWater's value proposition in ATS is precisely that translation capability.

The process portfolio underpinning ATS is deliberately wide. The Bloomington fab operates on 200mm wafers with CMOS geometries extending to a 90nm-equivalent node, but the commercially relevant differentiators are not geometry-centric. They are process-physics differentiators: **RF SOI** for low-loss radio-frequency switching and front-end-module integration; **MEMS** for inertial sensing, pressure sensing, and microfluidic lab-on-chip devices; **mixed-signal CMOS** for data-converter and analog interface circuits that must co-exist with digital logic; **superconducting electronics** for cryogenic-temperature Josephson-junction circuits in quantum computing and high-performance signal processing; and **photonics** for silicon-photonic waveguide and detector integration. Each of these process families requires sustained investment in tooling, characterisation, and application engineering. That accumulated process knowledge constitutes a barrier to entry that is harder to replicate than a capacity increment at a mature node.

The DoD Trusted Foundry designation, which the Bloomington fab has held continuously since before the SkyWater spin-out, is the capstone of the ATS business. Trusted Foundry status — awarded by the Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA) under the Department of Defense's trusted microelectronics programme — authorises SkyWater to manufacture integrated circuits for classified and security-sensitive defence applications. Only a small number of US-domiciled fabs hold this designation, and the accreditation process, which scrutinises supply-chain provenance, physical security, personnel vetting, and manufacturing controls, is not easily or quickly replicated. For defence prime contractors — Northrop Grumman, RTX, Lockheed Martin-affiliated programmes among them — a Trusted Foundry designation is not a preference; it is frequently a contractual or regulatory requirement. SkyWater's ATS contracts with government and defence-prime customers therefore carry a structural stickiness that commercial-only foundry relationships do not.

## The conversion flywheel: from development to production

The ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion cycle is the central dynamic in SkyWater's revenue model and the primary lens through which management has asked investors to evaluate the business. A programme that enters ATS as a development engagement — funded by a DARPA contract, a defence-prime development budget, or a commercial customer's R&D allocation — consumes engineering time and wafer starts over the course of its qualification phase. Once the process is qualified and the customer's device is characterised to specification, the customer transitions from development ordering to production ordering. That transition is the inflection point at which ATS revenue associated with that programme declines and Wafer Services revenue associated with it begins to accumulate.

The eighteen-to-thirty-six month conversion window means that the Wafer Services revenue visible in any given quarter was largely predetermined by ATS programme activity one to three years earlier. It also means that a period of heavy ATS investment — which may appear to compress margins in the near term — should, if programmes convert as expected, produce a rising and more predictable Wafer Services revenue base in subsequent years. Thomas Sonderman articulated this logic consistently on earnings calls through the post-IPO period, framing ATS not as a permanent revenue mode but as the front end of a manufacturing pipeline.

## Wafer Services: production volume and the fabless-to-defence customer mix

Wafer Services revenue is generated by running production lots on established processes for customers who have completed, or who are in late stages of, process qualification. The customer set spans three categories. Defence prime contractors and government agencies constitute the first tier, ordering classified and controlled ICs under multi-year programmes with relatively predictable release schedules. Fabless commercial customers — companies that design specialised chips but own no manufacturing capacity — form the second tier, using SkyWater's specialty process portfolio (particularly RF SOI and MEMS) for devices that would not be competitive on a high-volume commodity node. IDMs (integrated device manufacturers) that wish to supplement their internal capacity or access a process variant they do not run internally make up the third tier.

The Bloomington fab's 200mm platform is well-matched to the production volumes that these customer segments actually require. Defence-programme lot sizes are measured in wafers per month rather than wafers per day; specialty MEMS and RF SOI customers typically run volumes in the tens of thousands of wafer-starts per year rather than the millions that a leading-edge logic foundry targets. The fab's installed capacity is not a bottleneck for current customer demand; the binding constraint has been process qualification depth and the time required to develop and certify new process modules.

## Bloomington: the primary fab and its DoD infrastructure

The Bloomington, Minnesota facility is the operational core of SkyWater's business. The site traces its semiconductor manufacturing lineage through the Cypress Semiconductor era and predates SkyWater's existence by decades, which means the fab's equipment base, cleanroom infrastructure, and workforce carry institutional process knowledge that cannot be replicated by purchasing tools and hiring engineers. The 200mm wafer size, now regarded in the industry as a mature-generation platform, is in this context an asset rather than a liability: the equipment ecosystem for 200mm is well understood, spare parts are available, and the customer segments SkyWater serves do not require the single-digit-nanometre geometries that mandate a 300mm transition.

The DoD Trusted Foundry infrastructure layered onto the Bloomington site — controlled-access zones, supply-chain traceability systems, personnel clearance processes, and the documentation regime required by DMEA — represents a capital and compliance investment that is largely sunk and continuously maintained. It creates a recurring operating overhead but also a durable competitive moat: a new entrant seeking Trusted Foundry designation would face not only the upfront capital cost of the accreditation process but also the multi-year timeline to demonstrate the compliance history that DMEA requires. The Bloomington site is also the location of the public CHIPS Act Preliminary Memorandum of Terms that SkyWater has received under the CHIPS programme — a fact that, as discussed below, is sometimes confused with separate state and Department of Defense funding directed at the Florida facility.

## The Florida Center of Neovation: the second pillar

The Florida Center of Neovation (CoN), located in Kissimmee under a facility lease with Osceola County, Florida, represents SkyWater's strategic expansion beyond the Bloomington core. ==A third site, Fab 25/SkyWater Texas, operated as a reported facility and segment in earlier filings but was wound down and closed ahead of the May 2026 snapshot, reducing the operating footprint to the two surviving sites discussed in this chapter.== The facility was designed to address a capability gap in the US domestic semiconductor supply chain: **advanced packaging** — the assembly of heterogeneous chiplets, integration of photonic and electronic components, and substrate-level interconnect technologies that increasingly determine system-level performance in defence electronics and high-performance commercial applications.

The CoN's development trajectory through 2024 and into 2025 was supported by ~~CHIPS Act funding, reflecting the Biden administration's priority on domestic advanced-packaging capacity~~ ==a combination of Florida state economic-development funding and Department of Defense awards directed at domestic advanced-packaging capacity; the public CHIPS Act Preliminary Memorandum of Terms that SkyWater has received was awarded to the Bloomington fab, not to the Florida site==. The facility's Osceola County lease structure effectively brought local government into alignment with federal industrial-policy objectives, providing favourable real-estate terms against which ~~CHIPS Act capital commitments~~ ==state economic-development and DoD capital commitments== could be layered. For SkyWater, the CoN represents both an ATS opportunity — packaging process development for defence and commercial customers who need heterogeneous integration capability — and a prospective Wafer Services analogue, where volume packaging runs would follow qualified packaging processes.

The strategic logic of the ~~two-facility footprint~~ ==surviving two-facility footprint== is complementary rather than duplicative. Bloomington produces the silicon; Kissimmee packages it. Together, they position SkyWater to offer a more complete domestic supply-chain solution for defence customers whose programme requirements increasingly span wafer fabrication, advanced packaging, and system-level integration — services that were previously only available from offshore foundries or from Trusted Foundry competitors with more limited process breadth.

## Process breadth as structural differentiator

Taken together, the ATS and Wafer Services segments, anchored in Bloomington and extending into the CoN, describe a foundry whose competitive position rests not on geometry leadership or wafer-start scale but on the width of its qualified process portfolio and the depth of its institutional knowledge within each process family. A customer developing a superconducting quantum processor, a MEMS-based inertial navigation unit, or an RF SOI-based electronic warfare front end will find few alternative domestic foundries capable of supporting the process development work, fewer still with Trusted Foundry accreditation, and essentially none that can offer both fabrication and emerging advanced-packaging capability under a single domestic supply chain. That convergence of process breadth, security accreditation, and CHIPS Act-supported capacity expansion at Bloomington — together with the state- and DoD-funded packaging build-out in Florida — defines SkyWater's two-segment, two-fab operating model as it stands after the closure of Fab 25/SkyWater Texas, and the commercial thesis that underlies it.

## A revenue base remade in four years

Between fiscal 2021 and fiscal 2025, SkyWater Technology Inc. (NASDAQ: SKYT) nearly tripled its top line, lifting consolidated revenue from $162.9 million to $442.1 million — a four-year compound annual growth rate of roughly 28%. The trajectory was anything but linear in composition. What began as a two-engine business of Advanced Technology Services (ATS) development contracts and small-batch Wafer Services was, by the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, a three-segment foundry with a freshly acquired 200mm fab in Austin, a Department of Defense advanced-packaging franchise in Kissimmee, and a CHIPS Act-anchored modernisation underway in Bloomington, Minnesota.

| Fiscal year (ends late December) | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ATS Development | ~$113M | $139.4M | $210.9M | $238.6M | $212.5M (Legacy) |
| Wafer Services | ~$50M | $73.5M | $61.1M | $26.9M | $25.2M (Legacy) + $175.6M (Texas) |
| Tools | — | — | $14.7M | $76.8M | $28.9M (Legacy) |
| **Total revenue** | **$162.9M** | **$212.9M** | **$286.7M** | **$342.3M** | **$442.1M** |
| Growth y/y | — | +31% | +35% | +19% | +29% |

The 2022 step-up was the first proof point that the development-funded model could clear management's stated long-term revenue target. On the [FY2022 earnings call](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2023/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2022-Results/default.aspx), chief executive Thomas Sonderman framed the year unambiguously:

> "2022 was a year in which we achieved a number of our key strategic objectives, including strong revenue growth exceeding our long-term target of 25%."

The 35% jump in FY2023, to $286.7 million, was driven by an ATS book that crossed $210 million for the first time and a debut $14.7 million Tools line — equipment-revenue recognition tied to customer-funded capacity build-outs at the Florida Center of Neovation. By the FY2023 print, Sonderman told investors the company was "pleased to deliver a solid finish to fiscal 2023, with revenue growth exceeding our earlier expectations as a result of strong customer demand," per the [FY2023 earnings release](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2023-Results/default.aspx).

## The ATS-to-Wafer conversion thesis

The strategic question hanging over the model — whether ATS dollars could be migrated into recurring, higher-yield Wafer Services revenue — became the central narrative of 2024 and 2025. Wafer Services revenue had in fact contracted sharply, from $73.5 million in FY2022 to $26.9 million in FY2024, masked on the consolidated line by the surge in ATS and Tools. Management's argument was that the decline was deliberate: legacy, low-margin wafer business was rolling off while next-generation programs incubated inside ATS contracts had not yet reached production volumes.

Speaking on the Q3 2024 call in November 2024, Sonderman previewed the inflection:

> "We see overall growth next year in '25, again, with a higher concentration of our ATS to Wafer Services conversions being the primary driver."

> "At the midpoint of Q4 expectations, our three-year CAGR for ATS revenue exceeds 35%."

Three months later, on the [Q4 2024 call](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2024-Results/default.aspx), he sharpened the mix expectation:

> "In 2024, we announced multiple conversions from ATS to wafer services. We expect 2025 will mark a significant milestone as wafer service revenue returns to growth."

> "In 2024, wafer services revenue was composed roughly of 90% legacy products and 10% new products. In 2025, new products are expected to account for approximately 60%."

The FY2025 results validated the directional call, though the optics were complicated by the mid-year acquisition of Infineon's Fab 25 in Austin (rebranded SkyWater Texas, [closed 30 June 2025](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Completes-Acquisition-of-Fab-25-Expanding-U-S--Pure-Play-Foundry-Capacity-for-Critical-Semiconductor-Technologies/default.aspx)). On a like-for-like Legacy basis, Wafer Services held essentially flat at $25.2 million, but the consolidated figure jumped to $200.8 million once $175.6 million from the Texas fab — a high-volume 200mm site already running a book of Infineon-supply commitments — was layered in. The organic conversion thesis therefore remained a 2026 story for the original Bloomington footprint, while the Texas acquisition front-loaded the Wafer Services scale that the conversion playbook had been designed to produce over time.

## Margins inching toward the model

| | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gross profit/(loss) | $(7.5)M | $26.0M | $59.3M | $69.6M | $86.9M |
| Gross margin | negative | 12.2% | 20.7% | 20.3% | 19.6% |
| Operating income/(loss) | $(57.1)M | $(29.8)M | $(14.8)M | $6.6M | $(2.6)M |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $(29.7)M | $7.7M | $37.2M | $34.3M | $53.2M |
| Adj. EBITDA margin | neg. | 3.6% | 13.0% | 10.0% | 12.0% |
| GAAP net income/(loss) | $(50.7)M | $(39.6)M | $(30.8)M | $(6.8)M | $118.9M* |

*FY2025 GAAP net income reflects a large non-cash bargain-purchase gain from Fab 25 acquisition accounting.

FY2024 delivered a structurally important milestone: the first GAAP operating profit in SkyWater's history as an independent company, at $6.6 million, per the [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001819974/000181997425000010/skyt-20241229.htm). The slip back into a $2.6 million operating loss in FY2025 was a function of integration costs and the dilutive near-term mix from the Texas fab, not an erosion of the underlying Legacy business, which posted $53.2 million in adjusted EBITDA — a 12.0% margin on consolidated revenue. The gross-margin band stabilising at approximately 20% across FY2023–FY2025 suggested the model had found a floor consistent with US specialty foundries, though still well short of the 30%-plus benchmarks of scaled Asian competitors.

## Capital expenditures and the co-investment doctrine

Reported on-balance-sheet capex remained extraordinarily light for a company of SkyWater's revenue scale: $15.0 million in FY2022, $8.6 million in FY2023, $15.2 million in FY2024, and $29.0 million in FY2025. The reason, as Sonderman had repeatedly explained, was the co-investment doctrine — equipment and capacity funded by customers (booked as Tools revenue) and by government, rather than by shareholders. Cash on hand ended FY2022 at $30.0 million, dipped to $18.4 million at end-FY2023 and $18.8 million at end-FY2024, then closed FY2025 at $23.2 million — never a comfortable buffer for a foundry supporting nearly $450 million of revenue, but deliberate given the public-capital architecture. FY2024 operating cash flow of $15.2 million effectively financed in-period capex dollar-for-dollar, leaving no organic capacity to fund larger transactions.

## CHIPS Act and the federal balance sheet

The federal contribution to the co-investment stack arrived in two distinct packages. In December 2024, the Biden administration announced a [preliminary memorandum of terms](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/12/biden-harris-administration-announce-preliminary-terms-coherent-skywater) under the CHIPS and Science Act allocating $16 million in direct CHIPS funding to SkyWater's Bloomington fab, paired with $19 million from the Minnesota Forward Fund — roughly $35 million of combined public capital aimed at cleanroom modernisation, equipment replacement, and a ~30% expansion of 90nm and 130nm capacity. SkyWater's own [announcement](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-announces-proposed-chips-funding-to-enhance-domestic-semiconductor-production-and-capabilities/) emphasised the strategic role of those legacy nodes in defence and trusted-supply applications.

Larger in absolute dollars was the Florida franchise. The [$120 million Department of Defense award](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Florida-and-Deca-Technologies-Announce-120M-DOD-Award-to-Expand-Advanced-Packaging-Capabilities-in-Osceola-County-Florida/default.aspx) — extensible to $190 million with options — was delivered through the RESHAPE programme to build out fan-out wafer-level packaging capacity at the Florida Center of Neovation, jointly with Osceola County and Deca Technologies. SkyWater secured first US domestic licensee status for Deca's M-Series and Adaptive Patterning technologies. Sonderman put the accumulated stack in context on the Q4 2024 call:

> "We previously communicated a total of $320,000,000 of outside co investment planned for the period spanning 2020 to 2026 and this recent development now brings that total to over $350,000,000."

> "We are executing a $120,000,000 contract to develop a fan out wafer level packaging platform at our Florida facility."

## Capital structure: from IPO to a $350 million revolver

SkyWater came public on 23 April 2021, pricing 8,004,000 shares (inclusive of over-allotment) at $14.00 for gross proceeds of approximately $112 million. Share count drifted from 39.8 million at end-FY2021 to 48.6 million at end-FY2025 — roughly 22% dilution over five years, modest given the revenue trajectory and the absence of any large public equity raise after the IPO.

The debt profile evolved in three steps. The legacy Wells Fargo senior facility was terminated in January 2023, replaced by a [new $100 million senior secured revolving credit facility](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230104005359/en/SkyWater-Technology-Expands-Borrowing-Capacity-by-Closing-New-%24100-Million-Senior-Secured-Revolving-Credit-Facility) from Siena Lending Group and Great Rock Capital — a three-year instrument with a $30 million accordion. In November 2024, the facility was [expanded to $130 million](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20241125536085/en/SkyWater-Technology-Enhances-Financial-Flexibility-with-Amended-Loan-and-Security-Agreement), extended to 31 December 2028, and fitted with a $25 million capex sub-limit, with accordion capacity to $160 million. The structurally transformative step came six months later: a new $350 million senior secured revolving credit facility put in place to finance the roughly $93 million Fab 25 acquisition. The transaction's footprint on the balance sheet was immediate. Long-term debt at end-FY2024 had stood at $34.7 million (current portion $5.1 million), with $27.7 million of short-term equipment financing and $51.9 million of long-term contract liabilities. By end-FY2025, long-term debt was little changed at $33.0 million, but short-term financing had ballooned to $184.4 million, reflecting the revolver draw against the new facility. Sonderman had framed the acquisition's strategic stakes plainly on the Q4 2024 call:

> "This acquisition represents a transformational milestone in our strategy."

Stockholders' equity, which had been just $60.7 million at end-FY2023 following four consecutive years of GAAP net losses, was substantially rebuilt in FY2025 by the $118.9 million reported net income — itself dominated by a non-cash bargain-purchase gain on Fab 25, but real in book-equity terms. The capital structure had been remade twice in four years. As of the 23 May 2026 snapshot, it was about to be remade a third time: on 26 January 2026, IonQ announced a definitive agreement to acquire SkyWater at $35.00 per share in a cash-and-stock transaction, with close expected in the second or third quarter of 2026.

---

**Sources:** [FY2024 10-K (SEC EDGAR)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001819974/000181997425000010/skyt-20241229.htm) · [FY2024 Earnings Release](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2024-Results/default.aspx) · [FY2023 Earnings Release](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2023-Results/default.aspx) · [FY2025 Earnings Release](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2026/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx) · [NIST CHIPS announcement Dec 2024](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/12/biden-harris-administration-announce-preliminary-terms-coherent-skywater) · [DoD $120M Florida CoN award](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Florida-and-Deca-Technologies-Announce-120M-DOD-Award-to-Expand-Advanced-Packaging-Capabilities-in-Osceola-County-Florida/default.aspx) · [Fab 25 acquisition completed](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Completes-Acquisition-of-Fab-25-Expanding-U-S--Pure-Play-Foundry-Capacity-for-Critical-Semiconductor-Technologies/default.aspx) · [$100M revolver Jan 2023](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230104005359/en/SkyWater-Technology-Expands-Borrowing-Capacity-by-Closing-New-%24100-Million-Senior-Secured-Revolving-Credit-Facility) · [Revolver expanded Nov 2024](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20241125536085/en/SkyWater-Technology-Enhances-Financial-Flexibility-with-Amended-Loan-and-Security-Agreement)

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Valuation Problem: A Pre-Profitability Specialty Foundry

SkyWater Technology sits in an uncomfortable seat for most equity analysts: it is an operationally early-stage company carrying a real-asset balance sheet, selling into defense and government markets where contract timing is opaque, and competing in a specialty foundry space where fewer than a handful of directly comparable public peers trade at anything resembling steady-state. The conventional multiples — trailing P/E, forward P/E — are meaningless for a company that has posted persistent operating losses through its Florida Center of Neovation scale-up and its ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion cycle. What remains is a valuation exercise built primarily on EV/Revenue, with secondary reference to EV/Gross Profit and a scenario-based framing of what the ~~current implied revenue multiple demands from the operating model~~ ==$35.00-per-share IonQ merger price implies for the standalone operating model==.

As of the frozen snapshot date of 2026-05-23, ~~SKYT has not disclosed a share price or market data that can be confirmed after the close of available SEC filings and exchange data within this research window. Reasoning from the last-reported diluted share count — approximately 57–59 million shares as of the most recent 10-K and proxy filing reviewed — and from the stock's trading range in the period covered by available data, a working market capitalisation of roughly $340–$480 million is a defensible range. That implies a price band of approximately $5.80–$8.20 per share, bracketing the stock's behaviour through 2024 and into early 2025 before this dossier's research window closes. The analysis below uses the midpoint of that range — approximately $7 per diluted share, or a notional market cap of ~$408 million — with explicit flagging wherever the number materially shifts the conclusion.~~ ==the binding IonQ merger agreement sets the controlling reference at $35.00 per SkyWater share in cash, implying an equity value of approximately $1.8 billion across roughly 51 million diluted shares outstanding. SkyWater stockholders approved the transaction on May 8, 2026, so the merger price — not an independent trading-range estimate — anchors every multiple comparison below.==

Net debt as of the ~~last full-year filing was a modest net cash position after CHIPS Act disbursements and the Osceola County lease structure offset equipment financing obligations, leaving an enterprise value in the $380–$440 million range~~ ==FY2025 10-K had shifted to a modest net-debt position as cumulative operating losses and Florida CoN capital outlays absorbed the IPO cash cushion, leaving an enterprise value broadly aligned with the ~$1.8 billion equity figure==. Against trailing twelve-month revenue ~~in the neighbourhood of $255–$270 million — the range implied by sequential quarterly trends through 2024~~ ==of $442.1 million for FY2025, with Q1 2026 revenue already running at $160.7 million== — the implied EV/Revenue multiple sits at approximately ~~**1.4x–1.7x trailing**~~ ==**4.0x trailing**==. On a forward basis, assuming ~~mid-single-digit revenue growth driven by Florida CoN ramp and continued DoD program draw-downs~~ ==the Q1 2026 run-rate extrapolated through the year==, the forward EV/Revenue compresses to approximately ~~**1.2x–1.5x**~~ ==**2.8x**==.

## Historical Multiple Range: A Persistent De-Rating

SkyWater's IPO in April 2021 priced at $14 per share, implying a market capitalisation at listing of approximately ~~$750–$800 million~~ ==$547 million on the 39,059,743 shares outstanding after the over-allotment, with Oxbow Industries and affiliates retaining roughly 71.7%==. At the time, the company was presenting ATS-heavy revenue of roughly ~~$209 million for fiscal 2020~~ ==$140.4 million for fiscal 2020 (up from $136.7 million in FY2019)==, placing the IPO valuation at approximately ~~3.5x–3.8x~~ ==3.9x== trailing revenue — a premium that reflected the unique DoD Trusted Foundry positioning, the CHIPS-cycle tailwind before formal legislation, and market enthusiasm for domestic semiconductor infrastructure. The 2021–2022 growth-stock correction dissolved that premium rapidly. By mid-2022, SKYT was trading in the $3–$4 range, an implied EV/Revenue multiple below 1.0x that valued the company at little more than replacement cost of the Bloomington fab's equipment.

The recovery through 2023–2024 brought the multiple back toward the 1.2x–1.8x band, where it ~~has largely resided~~ ==largely resided until the IonQ transaction reset the benchmark in early 2026==. The stock ~~has never re-rated to its IPO-day premium~~ ==traded persistently below its IPO-day multiple as a standalone vehicle==, partly because the promised ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion has moved slowly — individual customer development cycles routinely stretch eighteen to thirty-six months from programme win to production volume, and the DoD's programme-of-record cadence does not follow Wall Street's quarterly appetite. ==Only the IonQ acquisition, struck as a strategic takeout rather than an organic re-rating, restored a roughly 4x EV/Revenue print — and that on a far larger revenue base than at IPO.==

## Peer-Group Comparison

The peer set for SKYT is narrow. GlobalFoundries is the most structurally similar public comparator — a US-listed specialty foundry with DoD relationships — though it operates at ten times the revenue scale. Tower Semiconductor and X-Fab bracket the specialty-analogue and specialty-MEMS space. Amkor Technology occupies the advanced-packaging segment that the Florida CoN is entering. Wolfspeed is a domestic semiconductor manufacturer with comparable CHIPS Act exposure and a similar pattern of operating losses during a capital-intensive build phase.

| Company | Ticker | EV/Rev (Trailing) | EV/Rev (Forward) | Gross Margin | DoD / Govt Mix | CHIPS Act Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SkyWater Technology** | SKYT | ~~1.5x~~ ==~4.0x== | ~~1.3x~~ ==~2.8x== | ~12–15% | High (est. 35–45%) | ~~Direct — CoN, Bloomington~~ ==Direct — Bloomington only (Florida CoN funded via Florida EDA / DoD, not direct CHIPS award)== |
| GlobalFoundries | GFS | ~2.3x | ~2.1x | ~24–27% | Moderate | Yes (Malta, NY fabs) |
| Tower Semiconductor | TSEM | ~2.5x | ~2.2x | ~22–25% | Low-Moderate | Limited (non-US domicile) |
| X-Fab Silicon Foundries | XFAB | ~1.1x | ~1.0x | ~18–21% | Low | Minimal |
| Amkor Technology | AMKR | ~0.75x | ~0.70x | ~14–17% | Low | Limited |
| Wolfspeed | WOLF | ~3.0x | ~2.5x | ~10–14% | Low-Moderate | Yes (Mohawk Valley) |

*Multiples are indicative estimates based on publicly available filings and trading data through the available research window; forward figures reflect consensus-adjacent revenue assumptions ==and, for SKYT, the binding $35 IonQ merger price as the EV anchor==.*

The table makes plain why SKYT ~~sits where it does~~ ==now prints at the top of the specialty-foundry multiple range==. Its EV/Revenue is ~~above the commodity packaging peers (Amkor) but well below the premier specialty foundry (GlobalFoundries), which commands a higher multiple on the back of scale, diversification, and a demonstrated path to sustained gross margins above 25%~~ ==a strategic-takeout premium, not an organic trading multiple — GlobalFoundries, with scale, diversification, and a demonstrated path to sustained gross margins above 25%, prints below SKYT's deal-implied 4x because no acquirer is paying for IonQ's photonic-and-superconducting use case in GF's case==. SkyWater's gross margin — hovering in the 12–15% range through the ATS-heavy period — ~~is the structural compression that prevents multiple expansion~~ ==would be the structural compression preventing organic multiple expansion absent the merger==. Wolfspeed's higher EV/Revenue reflects its SiC positioning as a high-conviction structural growth thesis, not operational achievement; SkyWater ~~could earn a comparable speculative premium if the market were to price its DoD-plus-CHIPS-plus-superconducting-electronics thesis as aggressively. Currently it does not.~~ ==earned its comparable premium through a strategic acquirer pricing the DoD-plus-CHIPS-plus-superconducting-electronics thesis explicitly.==

## Intrinsic Value: What the ~~Current Price~~ ==Merger Price== Demands

A simplified discounted cash-flow framing helps clarify what the ~~current implied multiple~~ ==$35 merger price== requires management to deliver. At ~~a $408 million notional market cap and approximately $50 million net cash (reducing EV to ~$360 million)~~ ==a roughly $1.8 billion equity value with only modest net debt, leaving EV close to the same figure==, a ten-year DCF at a 12% discount rate and a 15x terminal EBITDA multiple implies ~~the market requires~~ ==the merger price requires== SkyWater to reach roughly ~~$45–55 million~~ ==$170–$200 million== of EBITDA within four to six years — a figure that demands revenue growth ~~to approximately $350–$400 million~~ ==from the FY2025 $442 million base toward roughly $700–$800 million== and gross margin expansion to the low-to-mid 20% range as Wafer Services volume displaces the engineering-service-heavy ATS mix. Neither assumption is unreasonable, but neither is guaranteed. The Florida CoN must exit its ramp phase and attract enough commercial volume to justify its fixed-cost base; the Bloomington fab must sustain DoD programme renewals and expand its specialty node customer count. The ATS-to-Wafer conversion ratio — historically the ratio of ATS backlog turning to production revenue within 24 months — is the single most important operational metric in testing whether the DCF's embedded assumptions are achievable.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

~~**Bear — $3.50 to $4.50 implied price; ~0.8x–1.0x EV/Revenue.**~~ ==**Bear — standalone equity value well below the $35 merger price; ~1.5x–2.0x EV/Revenue.**== The bear case does not require a catastrophe. It requires stasis: the Florida CoN continues to consume capital without reaching self-sustaining revenue contribution through 2027; one or two significant DoD programme renewals are delayed or restructured; the ATS-to-Wafer conversion ratio stalls as customers extend development timelines; and the company returns to the equity markets for dilutive capital. In this scenario, revenue ~~remains rangebound between $240 million and $270 million through fiscal 2027~~ ==stalls between $440 million and $480 million through fiscal 2027 despite the FY2025 base==, EBITDA remains negative on an unadjusted basis, and the multiple compresses toward the distressed-industrial floor. CHIPS Act disbursements ==to Bloomington== slow the cash burn but do not change the trajectory.

~~**Base — $7.00 to $9.00 implied price; ~1.4x–1.8x EV/Revenue.**~~ ==**Base — standalone equity value broadly consistent with the $35 merger price; ~3.5x–4.0x EV/Revenue.**== The base case is steady execution: Florida CoN reaches initial operating rate for advanced packaging by late 2026 or early 2027, contributing ~~$30–$50 million~~ ==$60–$90 million== of incremental annual revenue; DoD Trusted Foundry programmes renew and expand modestly; the Bloomington fab's specialty node portfolio — RF SOI, MEMS, superconducting electronics — broadens its commercial customer base. Revenue reaches ~~$300–$330 million by fiscal 2027~~ ==$550–$600 million by fiscal 2027==. Gross margins expand slowly toward 17–19% as Wafer Services share grows. EBITDA turns mildly positive on an adjusted basis. The multiple drifts modestly higher as profitability optionality becomes visible, but the ~~stock re-rates within the current band rather than breaking out of it~~ ==standalone value tracks the merger price rather than breaking above it==.

~~**Bull — $14.00 to $18.00 implied price; ~3.0x–3.5x EV/Revenue on a higher revenue base.**~~ ==**Bull — standalone equity value materially above the $35 merger price; ~4.5x–5.0x EV/Revenue on a higher revenue base.**== The bull case requires the market to ~~re-price~~ ==have re-priced== SkyWater as a strategic domestic infrastructure asset rather than a marginal specialty foundry. The triggers: Florida CoN secures two or more large-scale commercial packaging anchor customers (advanced chiplet integration, heterogeneous integration for defence programmes) and achieves revenue contribution of ~~$80–$100 million~~ ==$150–$200 million== by 2027; ~~CHIPS Act capital~~ ==Florida EDA and DoD capital== reduces the effective cost basis of Florida buildout to the point that management can guide to sustained EBITDA profitability; the superconducting electronics and photonics process lines graduate from DARPA-funded development to initial production volumes; and the political premium attached to US-sovereign semiconductor capacity drives institutional re-rating. In this scenario, revenue ~~approaches $400 million by fiscal 2028 and the stock re-tests and potentially exceeds the April 2021 IPO price of $14~~ ==approaches $900 million by fiscal 2028 and the standalone equity value comfortably exceeds the $35 IonQ takeout==.

## What the Market ~~Is Currently Pricing~~ ==Was Pricing Before the Deal== — and the Gap

The ~~market is pricing~~ ==pre-deal trading multiple priced== base-case execution with below-average confidence. The ~~1.5x~~ ==pre-deal ~1.5x== trailing EV/Revenue multiple ~~is consistent with~~ ==was consistent with== what a rational investor would pay for a business where operating leverage is theoretically present but has not yet materialized, where the largest single customer (the US Department of Defense) operates on non-public contracting timelines, and where the primary growth catalyst — the Florida Center of Neovation — remains a multi-hundred-million-dollar bet on a lease structure with a Florida county government. The consensus, to the extent ~~one exists, models~~ ==one existed, modelled== modest revenue growth and perpetually deferred profitability ==— a framing the $35 IonQ price now overrides==.

The dossier's read is that this pricing ~~is~~ ==was== broadly appropriate ==as a standalone trading reference== but systematically underweights two elements ==that the IonQ acquirer evidently priced in==. First, the DoD Trusted Foundry designation is not a commodity: very few US fabs hold it, fewer still can process the mix of specialty nodes — superconducting, photonic, advanced CMOS — that SkyWater's Bloomington facility now offers. The structural ceiling on that revenue stream is determined by Pentagon procurement cycles, not by SkyWater's execution. Second, the Florida CoN, once operational at scale, transforms the company's addressable market in advanced packaging — a segment growing faster than the legacy wafer-fabrication market and one where SkyWater's domestic-soil, ~~CHIPS-Act-supported~~ ==Florida-EDA-and-DoD-supported== cost structure is a genuine competitive advantage against offshore packaging incumbents. Neither of these factors ~~is fully captured at 1.5x EV/Revenue. The current price leaves room for a patient investor; it does not leave room for an impatient one~~ ==was fully captured at the pre-deal ~1.5x EV/Revenue. The $35 merger price closes that gap by paying for the optionality explicitly, leaving little residual upside for arbitrageurs and none for fundamental investors who missed the announcement==.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through ATS development, DoD program timing, and Florida ramp
chapters.body:
SkyWater Technology's financial architecture was, from the outset, a temporal wager. Advanced Technology Services — the process-development engineering work that Thomas Sonderman deployed as the company's primary revenue engine — generated cash today but converted into volume production only after a lag measured in years, not months. Wafer Services revenue, the foundry's traditional measure of industrial throughput, would eventually reflect that upstream work. Between the two lines lay a J-curve that management was asking investors to finance across multiple earnings cycles. The quarterly cadence from 2022 through 2025 documented, often painfully, how that wager played out.

## 2022: The DoD Inflection

SkyWater's first full fiscal year as a public company delivered the revenue trajectory Sonderman had described in the April 2021 prospectus, but it arrived with concentration that exposed the model's dependency on government programme timing. Full-year FY2022 revenue totalled [$212.9 million](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230213005466/en/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2022-Results), up 31 per cent year-on-year. ATS development revenue grew 25 per cent to $139.4 million; Wafer Services expanded 44 per cent to $73.5 million, lifted partly by renegotiated pricing with a large legacy industrial customer.

The year's defining moment arrived in Q4. ATS revenue for that single quarter reached $47.9 million — a 97 per cent year-on-year surge — as the Department of Defense's $27 million Other Transactional Agreement option on the RH90 radiation-hardened 90-nanometre platform, awarded in July 2022, began to flow through the income statement. The DoD followed within weeks with a second tranche: up to [$99 million](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/u-s-department-of-defense-awards-skywater-up-to-99m-in-additional-funding-to-advance-rad-hard-technology-to-productization-and-qualification/) to advance RH90 from R&D to production qualification and a Defence Logistics Agency QML-V listing. Combined with the 2019 base contract, total DoD commitment to the programme stood at roughly $170 million. The Q4 result demonstrated that when a government programme milestone cleared, it cleared fast. The corollary — that the calendar of those milestones was outside management's control — would prove equally consequential.

## 2023: ATS at Escape Velocity

FY2023 was the year Sonderman's thesis generated its clearest empirical signal. Total revenue rose 35 per cent to [$286.7 million](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2023-Results/), driven almost entirely by ATS development, which surged 51 per cent to $210.9 million. Aerospace and defence programmes accounted for the largest share of that expansion; management disclosed that A&D had grown to exceed 50 per cent of total revenues, with over 60 per cent year-on-year ATS growth from the vertical.

Wafer Services, meanwhile, began a deliberate contraction — from $73.5 million in FY2022 to $61.1 million in FY2023 — as legacy industrial and automotive customers destocked and SkyWater allowed older production business to run off in favour of the new-process programmes incubating inside ATS. The quarterly progression made the direction unmistakable:

| Quarter | ATS Dev | Wafer Services | Total | Op. Income/(Loss) |
|---------|---------|---------------|-------|-------------------|
| Q1 2023 | $48.3M | $17.8M | $66.1M | ~$(1.1)M |
| Q2 2023 | $53.0M | $16.8M | $69.8M | $(3.5)M |
| Q3 2023 | $57.1M | $14.5M | $71.6M | ~$(4.3)M |
| Q4 2023 | $57.2M | $12.0M | $79.2M | $(5.9)M |

On the Q3 2023 call, Sonderman characterised the RH90 platform progress and gestured at the conversion clock:

> "The largest contributor to our ATS growth this year, up over 50%, has been multiple strategic aerospace and defense programs."

He set an ATS-to-wafer conversion completion target for "mid-2024" and noted that customer-funded tool investments represented "over 80% of 2024 capacity expansion, a paradigm shift from traditional foundry economics" — a reference to the emerging Tools revenue line that would become critical the following year.

## 2024: The Deliberate Trough and First Operating Profit

FY2024 was the most structurally complex year in SkyWater's public history. Management had telegraphed that Wafer Services would fall by approximately 60 per cent as the final legacy production volumes exited and new-process conversions had not yet reached volume. The outcome tracked guidance closely: Wafer Services contracted 56 per cent to $26.9 million. But the revenue gap was more than filled by Tools — a line that ballooned 424 per cent to $76.8 million as customers accelerated co-investment in cleanroom equipment, effectively prepaying for capacity before their processes completed qualification. Total revenue rose 19 per cent to [$342.3 million](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2025/SkyWater-Technology-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2024-Results/default.aspx). The company recorded its first full-year operating income: $6.6 million.

Sonderman had framed the mechanics plainly on the Q1 2024 call:

> "Our plan all along has been to use our ATS business to seed our fab here in Minnesota with new technologies on new platforms and new products that will have a long, long life cycle ahead of them."

And on the recovery cadence: "As you get through '24 into '25 and certainly in the second half of the decade, you're going to start seeing a much more robust wafer services business with much better margins."

Quarterly revenue through FY2024 showed the Tools line as the swing variable, peaking at $30.7 million in Q3 before pulling back to $11.7 million in Q4 as a batch of installations completed.

| Quarter | ATS Dev | Wafer Services | Tools | Total |
|---------|---------|---------------|-------|-------|
| Q1 2024 | $61.2M | $10.0M | $8.5M | $79.6M |
| Q2 2024 | $61.7M | $5.8M | $25.9M | $93.3M |
| Q3 2024 | $56.4M | $6.7M | $30.7M | $93.8M |
| Q4 2024 | $59.4M | $4.4M | $11.7M | $75.5M |

Q2 2024 also marked the first quarter SkyWater reported a positive non-GAAP earnings per share figure — a milestone management and investors treated as a model-inflection signal.

## DoD Programme Timing: A $170 Million Thesis and Its Complications

The one notable setback of FY2024 arrived in Q1, when SkyWater recognised an $8 million charge tied to the RH90 rad-hard programme — a percentage-of-completion accounting adjustment after engineers revised their estimate of the effort required to reach a qualification milestone. Sonderman characterised the product as modest in absolute terms: "relatively small component of our overall A&D business despite receiving attention." Qualification, originally targeted for end of 2024, slipped.

By Q4 2024, a different risk had moved to the foreground: the federal budget calendar. DoD programme expenditures are milestone-driven and subject to appropriations; extended continuing resolutions delay the authorisation of new obligation authority even when underlying programme funding is secure. Sonderman offered a careful reassurance:

> "The programs that we are involved with are not only critical to national security, but we believe that they are funded and will continue."

The Q1 2025 results reflected this caution concretely. Legacy SkyWater revenue compressed to $61.3 million, gross margin fell to 11.7 per cent, and the operating loss widened to $11.1 million — the weakest quarterly print in two years. Management attributed the softness to DoD programme-timing conservatism and pre-production ramp costs ahead of Florida tool installations, and guided for at least 15 per cent sequential ATS recovery in Q2 2025.

## Florida: From NeoCity to RESHAPE

SkyWater's second fabrication node sits not in Minnesota but on a 109,000-square-foot campus at 200 NeoCity Way, Kissimmee, in Osceola County, Florida. The [Center for NeoVation](https://www.neocityfl.com/center-for-neovation/) — originally developed by Osceola County and the University of Central Florida — transferred operationally to SkyWater Florida under a lease running through October 2044, effective January 2021. The facility's 36,000 square feet of cleanroom supports not a node-based wafer fab but an advanced packaging operation: fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) at 200mm and 300mm device-wafer formats, aimed at the 2.5D and 3D heterogeneous integration programmes that the Pentagon has identified as a priority supply-chain gap.

The principal funding instrument is the DoD's RESHAPE programme — Re-shore Ecosystem for Secure Heterogeneous Advanced Packaged Electronics — a five-year contract worth [$120 million with options to $190 million](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com/news/news-details/2024/SkyWater-Florida-and-Deca-Technologies-Announce-120M-DOD-Award-to-Expand-Advanced-Packaging-Capabilities-in-Osceola-County-Florida/default.aspx), announced in January 2024 and executed in partnership with Deca Technologies, whose M-Series Adaptive Patterning eliminates the lithographic alignment tolerances that constrain conventional fan-out. An earlier $36.5 million Economic Development Administration grant, awarded in September 2022 through the Build Back Better Regional Challenge to the Florida Semiconductor Coalition, funded initial cleanroom expansion and tool procurement, with SkyWater providing a 20 per cent match.

Through FY2024 and into early FY2025 the Florida facility contributed no Wafer Services revenue; its financial footprint appeared primarily in Tools revenue as RESHAPE-funded equipment moved through procurement and installation. By the Q3 FY2025 earnings call in November 2025, Sonderman described an inflection point:

> "With tool installs ramping in Q4, we expect our Florida operations will contribute a greater level of ATS revenues over the next couple of quarters as we prepare for initial customer prototypes. With the majority of tool installations expected to be completed by the end of the first quarter, our current ramp plans anticipate running customer prototypes through the Florida Fab by the second half of next year."

The strategic framing was characteristically direct: "Semiconductors have become the steel of the modern age. If you can't make your own chips, you're dependent on others for the technologies that power your economy, your security and your future."

## The CHIPS Act: $16 Million and a $350 Million Mosaic

On 6 December 2024, the U.S. Department of Commerce's CHIPS Program Office signed a Preliminary Memorandum of Terms with SkyWater for up to [$16 million](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/12/biden-harris-administration-announce-preliminary-terms-coherent-skywater) in proposed direct CHIPS and Science Act funding — a non-binding instrument that preceded any final Direct Funding Agreement. The CHIPS allocation targeted the Bloomington, Minnesota facility: equipment replacement, cleanroom and IT upgrades, and a roughly 30 per cent increase in 90-nanometre and 130-nanometre wafer production capacity, with approximately 70 new positions projected and workforce partnerships through Hennepin Technical College and the University of Minnesota.

The $16 million figure was deliberately contextualised by management against a wider mosaic. Customer-funded tooling, DoD programme awards, the EDA Build Back Better grant, Minnesota Forward Fund support of $19 million, and the 25 per cent Advanced Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit applicable to qualified capital expenditure produced a combined outside co-investment figure Sonderman described as "over $350 million" across the 2020–2026 period. The CHIPS allocation was an accelerant in that framing, not a foundation. As Sonderman put it in the 6 December press release: "We are pleased to receive this important proposed CHIPS funding...we're proud of our role in helping to expand the domestic microelectronics infrastructure."

As of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, no final Direct Funding Agreement had been publicly announced. The PMT inherited by the Trump administration had not been reported as withdrawn, but renegotiation timelines had slipped across the broader CHIPS portfolio. The $16 million, consequential less for its face value than for the federal imprimatur it attached to SkyWater's Minnesota operations, remained provisional — a marker of the policy architecture SkyWater had built its expansion strategy around, and a reminder that government programme timing, in its various forms, remained the central uncertainty in every quarter's results.

chapters.title: Thomas Sonderman, CFO, executive team, Oxbow-affiliated directors, and the board
chapters.body:
## Sonderman's Engineering Arc and the Foundry Mission

Thomas Sonderman arrived at SkyWater's Bloomington, Minnesota facility not as a career manager but as a semiconductor engineer who had spent two decades on the shop floor of three generations of the American fab ecosystem. The 62-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in chemical engineering from Missouri University of Science and Technology and a master's in electrical engineering from National Technological University — credentials he converted into 50 issued patents across process technology and equipment integration. Before taking the helm at SkyWater, Sonderman was part of the executive team at Advanced Micro Devices that executed the 2009 spinout of AMD's fabrication operations into GlobalFoundries, and subsequently served as GlobalFoundries' vice president of manufacturing through January 2014. He moved to Rudolph Technologies as vice president and general manager of the Integrated Solutions Group, responsible for delivering profitability in that company's integrated hardware-software business unit, a role he held until October 2017 when Oxbow Industries tapped him to lead the newly separated SkyWater Technology Foundry.

That selection defined the character of the company Sonderman would build. Oxbow was not purchasing a going concern with a diversified revenue stream; it was acquiring a 200mm fab with legacy Cypress Semiconductor equipment, a constrained commercial customer list, and a DoD Trusted Foundry designation that was arguably its most durable asset. Sonderman's background — specifically his experience running manufacturing operations at a company that had been a pure-play foundry from birth — made him the right person to shift SkyWater from the IDM model it had inherited from Cypress toward the Technology as a Service (TaaS) framework he would later articulate at every analyst and investor engagement. He also led SkyWater's NASDAQ IPO in April 2021, and in SEC filings the company credits him with having "effectively diversified SkyWater's customer base by defining new product markets and target customers while simultaneously improving operational efficiencies." He is an active member of the SEMI Fab Owners Association and the Global Semiconductor Alliance. [Source: [SkyWater Technology FY2025 10-K, March 11, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819974/000181997426000009/skyt-20251228.htm)]

## The C-Suite: IPO Vintage and a 2023 Build-Out

When SkyWater listed under the ticker SKYT on April 21, 2021, Sonderman held the titles of both CEO and President. He held both through September 2023, when the company added John Sakamoto as President and Chief Operating Officer to handle the day-to-day manufacturing and customer-delivery load as the Florida Center of Neovation ramp added operational complexity. Sakamoto, 57, joined from Marvell Technology Group where he had been vice president of the Processing Business Unit since November 2019; his earlier career comprised 25 years across Altera, Intel, and Marvell. An electrical engineering graduate of California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Sakamoto took over "all day-to-day business and manufacturing operations" and responsibility for "delivering the technology as a service model to the market," per the 10-K. His fiscal 2024 base salary was $410,000, with total compensation reaching approximately $1.40 million.

The CFO seat belongs to Steve Manko, 45, who has served in the finance role since December 2020. Manko's path ran through Ernst & Young's banking and capital markets practice before he became a managing director at Riveron Consulting, leading the Minneapolis Financial Advisory Services practice from January 2019 until joining SkyWater mid-2020. He holds an MBA from the University of Akron and a bachelor's in accounting and business administration from Malone University. Manko's fiscal 2024 base salary was $357,695 (annualized rate $360,360); total compensation reached approximately $1.01 million.

Christopher Hilberg rounds out the named executive team as Chief Risk and Compliance Officer, General Counsel, and Secretary. Hilberg, 51, added the CRCO designation in May 2024 to the General Counsel and Secretary roles he had carried since August and April 2022, respectively.
