A physics graduate of Carleton College and a JD from the University of Chicago Law School, Hilberg is a licensed patent attorney before the USPTO — expertise that proves particularly useful in a foundry where DoD Trusted Foundry program contracts and specialty-IP licensing routinely intersect.

The fiscal 2024 compensation cycle illustrated how performance expectations shaped executive pay. The compensation committee set a combined adjusted-EBITDA target of $40.5 million and a combined ATS-plus-Wafer-Services revenue target of $275.5 million as the hurdles for formulaic annual bonuses; neither target was achieved, producing zero plan-based bonus for all three named executives. The committee nonetheless voted discretionary bonuses — $272,950 to Sonderman, $153,750 to Sakamoto, and $99,099 to Manko — in recognition of individual contributions assessed after the year close. [Source: [SkyWater Technology DEF 14A, April 8, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819974/000114036125012823/ny20041354x1_def14a.htm)]

## The Board: Oxbow at the Centre

The single most structurally determinative fact about SkyWater's governance is the ownership position of CMI Oxbow Partners, LLC. As of the March 24, 2025 record date, with 48,034,573 shares outstanding, CMI Oxbow Partners held 11,160,832 shares (23.23% of common stock). Loren A. Unterseher, Managing Partner of Oxbow Industries and President of CMI Oxbow Partners, beneficially controlled 16,389,650 shares in aggregate — 34.11% of the company. The next-largest external holder was DDK Developments, LLC at 3,907,549 shares (8.13%). All directors and executive officers collectively held 18,438,624 shares (37.85%).

| Holder | Shares | % |
|---|---|---|
| CMI Oxbow Partners, LLC | 11,160,832 | 23.23% |
| Loren A. Unterseher (beneficial, incl. CMI Oxbow) | 16,389,650 | 34.11% |
| DDK Developments, LLC | 3,907,549 | 8.13% |
| Thomas Sonderman (incl. vested options) | 893,145 | 1.84% |
| Gary J. Obermiller | 489,114 | 1.02% |
| Steve Manko | 417,102 | \* |
| All directors and executives (12 persons) | 18,438,624 | 37.85% |

*Less than 1%.* [Source: [DEF 14A, April 8, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1819974/000114036125012823/ny20041354x1_def14a.htm)]

Unterseher, 60, has been a SkyWater director since October 2020. He has served as Managing Partner of Oxbow Industries — a Minneapolis-based holding company focused on middle-market private companies — since 2004, and as Managing Partner of Oxbow Realty Partners since September 2020. His career prior to Oxbow included M&A principal roles at Craig-Hallum Capital Group and Lazard Middle Market, and a vice president position in M&A at Royal Bank of Canada; before investment banking, he was a partner at Stinson Leonard Street LLP. He holds a BBA in Finance from the University of Iowa and a JD from the University of North Dakota.

Unterseher's multi-layered economic relationship with SkyWater extends well beyond share ownership. On September 29, 2020 — months before the IPO — SkyWater sold the land and building of its Bloomington primary facility to Oxbow Realty Partners in a transaction accounted for as a failed sale-leaseback: SkyWater retained the property on its balance sheet as a financing obligation while agreeing to monthly rent starting at $394,000 and escalating at 2% per year over a 20-year term ending September 2040. SkyWater paid Oxbow Realty $6.2 million in fiscal 2024; as of December 29, 2024, remaining future contractual payments totalled $89.9 million. Separately, Oxbow Industries holds a support agreement committing up to $12.5 million in liquidity backstop — originally signed August 2022, subsequently extended through March 2026 — of which no amounts had been drawn through fiscal 2024. A consulting agreement entered August 2023 embeds an Oxbow employee at SkyWater for a base monthly fee of $35,833, with performance fees of up to $1.2 million annually in fiscal 2024 and 2025 tied to production-cost reduction and weekly wafer-output targets.

## Independent Directors and the Defence Dimension

The nine-member board that took shape after the May 21, 2025 annual meeting balanced Oxbow's controlling influence with independent voices spanning semiconductor operations, defence logistics, finance, and public-sector leadership. Gregory Graves and Gary Obermiller — each long-serving independent directors, with Obermiller having served as non-executive chair — retired from the board at the meeting's conclusion.

The most operationally distinctive voice in the post-2023 period was General Edward M. Daly (ret.), who joined the board in October 2023. Daly, 59, spent 36 years in the U.S. Army, rising to Commanding General of Army Materiel Command from July 2020 until his retirement in May 2023 — a command encompassing 190,000 military, civilian, and contractor personnel, and the Army's primary materiel-fielding organisation worldwide, including logistics support for Ukraine. His appointment reflected the growing strategic weight of DoD Trusted Foundry production in SkyWater's revenue base and intensifying congressional attention to domestic semiconductor manufacturing security.

Nancy Fares, 58, brought complementary foundry credibility. A former VP of Operations at NXP Semiconductors who led advances in 3D packaging technology for multichip integration, Fares also served as President and CEO of Micralyne Inc., an independent semiconductor foundry — making her the board's closest structural analog to SkyWater's own business model. Her prior positions at Qualcomm (VP Software Product Management) and Texas Instruments added depth across the vertical.

Timothy Baxter, 64, assumed the non-executive chair role at the conclusion of the May 2025 annual meeting, succeeding Obermiller. An Operating Partner at Centre Partners Management and former President and CEO of Samsung Electronics North America — where he managed the company's long-term strategic plan for 5G, AI, and cloud — Baxter also chairs VueReal Inc., a MicroLED semiconductor company. Two further additions joined simultaneously: Andrew D. C. LaFrence, 62, CFO of Nortech Systems and a 26-year KPMG veteran whose background included contract manufacturing with US government contractors; and Tammy J. Miller, 65, former Lieutenant Governor of North Dakota (2023–2024) and former CEO of Border States Electric, where she served from 2006 to 2020. A CPA and MBA, Miller's appointment reflected the board's stated preference for diversified financial and public-sector expertise at a moment when the CHIPS Act had elevated government-relations capacity as a board competency.

## Compensation, Committees, and Transition

The 2025 proxy reflected an annual director compensation programme paying each non-employee director a $100,000 RSU grant upon election or re-election (vesting before the next annual meeting) plus cash retainers: a $65,000 base, supplemented by committee-chair fees of $15,000 for the audit chair, $10,000 for the compensation chair, $8,000 for the risk-management chair, and $5,000 for the nominating-and-governance chair. Unterseher received $85,000 in cash fees and the $100,000 RSU grant in fiscal 2024. Obermiller, as non-executive chair, received $123,000 in cash fees plus the same RSU grant.

A risk management committee — the board's newest standing committee — was established in August 2024, charged with overseeing strategic, operational, legal, regulatory, security, and technology risks including cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and privacy. Its creation coincided with the increased complexity of running simultaneous DoD Trusted Foundry production, a ~~CHIPS Act-supported Florida facility ramp~~ ==Florida facility ramp underwritten by Florida EDA and DoD funding (the public CHIPS PMT having been awarded for Bloomington, Minnesota rather than the Florida site)==, and a nascent superconducting-electronics development programme for DARPA.

On January 25, 2026, the board unanimously agreed to an Agreement and Plan of Merger with IonQ, Inc., the publicly traded quantum computing company, structured as a two-step merger in which IonQ would acquire SkyWater in its entirety. ~~The transaction remained subject to regulatory approvals and SkyWater stockholder consent as of the frozen snapshot date.~~ ==SkyWater stockholders approved the merger at a special meeting on May 8, 2026, leaving regulatory clearances as the only remaining gating items as of the frozen snapshot date.== For Sonderman, it represented the third foundry ownership transition of his career — from AMD to GlobalFoundries, from Cypress to SkyWater under Oxbow, and now toward IonQ's umbrella — each time as the operational technologist who built or rebuilt the manufacturing capability that made the transition strategically legible.

chapters.title: DoD Trusted Foundry, defense primes, DARPA/IARPA, fabless commercial customers
chapters.body:
## The Trusted Foundry Franchise

When the Department of Defense grants a semiconductor foundry its Trusted Foundry designation, it is not issuing a certification so much as installing a supply-chain firewall. The designation — administered through the Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA) — permits the manufacture of classified integrated circuits on US soil by a facility with cleared personnel operating under a security posture that commercial foundries based abroad cannot replicate. SkyWater Technology's Bloomington, Minnesota fab has held that designation continuously since before the 2017 spin-out from Cypress Semiconductor, and the inherited accreditation became the single most strategically durable asset Thomas Sonderman acquired when Oxbow Industries closed the transaction and handed him the keys to a 200mm fab on the prairie.

The designation functions as both a qualification barrier and a customer concentrator. Because defence programmes requiring DMEA-sanctioned production face a short list of eligible US-owned foundries, SkyWater competes against a structurally constrained set of alternatives — principally the IBM Microelectronics unit at Essex Junction (since acquired by GlobalFoundries) and, for older geometries, a handful of government-owned, contractor-operated facilities. That scarcity has meant that defence primes entering a new programme requiring a trusted-foundry process node have historically had limited negotiating leverage on the supply side. SkyWater's production volume for these customers is governed by long-cycle programme contracts, often spanning multiple years with milestone-based funding releases tied to defence acquisition schedules rather than commercial booking patterns.

## Defence Primes: Northrop, RTX, and the Lockheed Ecosystem

Among the defence prime contractors relying on SkyWater's Trusted Foundry capability, Northrop Grumman, RTX (formerly Raytheon Technologies), and Lockheed Martin-affiliated programmes have represented the principal production customers for classified and export-controlled IC fabrication through the 2022–2025 period. These relationships follow a common structural pattern: the prime holds the programme contract with a DoD acquisition office, a Tier-1 or Tier-2 electronics subsystem integrator specifies the IC requirement, and SkyWater sits at the fabrication layer, receiving design-rule-compliant GDSII layouts under controlled-unclassified or classified handling procedures and returning processed wafers and diced die under chain-of-custody protocols.

The specific programme affiliations are not disclosed in SkyWater's public filings beyond generic reference to defence customer revenue as a portion of total ATS and Wafer Services billings. What the 10-K filings do make clear is that defence-associated revenue has represented a material share of the company's total top line across the post-IPO period, and that programme timing — the periodic pause and restart rhythm intrinsic to the DoD acquisition cycle — has been a primary driver of quarterly revenue variability. A programme that enters a continuing resolution period or a programme-of-record review can compress wafer-starts authorisations at SkyWater with minimal commercial warning, a dynamic the company has flagged in its risk-factor disclosures since the April 2021 NASDAQ listing.

The Lockheed Martin-affiliated category spans not only direct Lockheed programmes but also work flowing through the Sandia National Laboratories and MIT Lincoln Laboratory supply chains, both of which route specialty semiconductor requirements through trusted-foundry channels. For SkyWater, these government laboratory customers sit at the intersection of the defence prime relationship and the DARPA/IARPA research customer base — a hybrid category that generates both ATS process-development billings and downstream Wafer Services production orders as laboratory prototypes mature into programme-of-record hardware.

## DARPA, IARPA, and the Government Research Customer Base

DARPA's Electronics Resurgence Initiative (ERI) and successor programmes have provided SkyWater with a recurring stream of funded process-development contracts that serve a dual commercial purpose: they accelerate node capability development at below-market engineering cost (because the government bears the NRE burden) while simultaneously seeding the ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion pipeline with future production-qualified processes.

Among the most technically distinctive of these engagements has been the DARPA-funded superconducting electronics programme, through which SkyWater has developed and refined a Josephson-junction process capable of supporting cryogenic computing architectures targeted at quantum computing adjacencies and ultra-low-power signal processing. The programme places SkyWater in a niche that no other US-owned foundry has fully replicated at production scale — a position that matters as the intelligence community's interest in post-CMOS computing substrates has intensified through the mid-2020s.

IARPA, the intelligence community's research funding arm, has also featured in SkyWater's customer base through programmes that mirror DARPA's structure: multi-phase, milestone-gated contracts that fund process development in Phase I with options to scale to prototype production in Phase II and III. The intelligence community's particular interest in radiation-hardened CMOS, photonic integrated circuits for secure communications, and mixed-signal sensor processing has aligned with the process portfolio that SkyWater accumulated through the Cypress Semiconductor era and has since extended through ATS investment.

The aggregate government research customer base — DARPA, IARPA, Air Force Research Laboratory, Office of Naval Research, and the DoE national laboratories — generates ATS revenue that carries engineering-service margin profiles distinct from commodity wafer pricing. Because these contracts fund personnel and equipment utilisation rather than simply wafer starts, they have helped SkyWater cover fixed-fab overhead during periods when production volumes were below full utilisation, functioning as a demand floor that purely commercial specialty foundries lack.

## Specialty Commercial Customers: RF SOI, MEMS, Mixed-Signal

Beyond the defence and government research vertical, SkyWater's commercial customer base has centred on fabless designers and integrated device manufacturers requiring specialty process nodes unavailable at the high-volume foundries that dominate the merchant market. Three process families have anchored this commercial franchise.

Radio-frequency silicon-on-insulator (RF SOI) process technology serves the mobile-infrastructure and satellite-communications customer segments, where the substrate's low-loss characteristics enable performance metrics — insertion loss, linearity, isolation — that bulk CMOS cannot match at comparable die area. SkyWater's RF SOI capability has attracted fabless customers designing front-end-module components for defence-adjacent communications hardware, a segment that benefits from the same Trusted Foundry supply-chain assurance as classified military programmes, since US government procurement offices increasingly require domestic-sourced RF components even for unclassified communications systems.

MEMS process capability has served customers in the aerospace sensing, medical device, and industrial instrumentation segments. The Bloomington fab's long history with surface and bulk micromachining processes — an inheritance from the Cypress-era MEMS customer relationships — has allowed SkyWater to offer co-integration of MEMS structures with CMOS readout circuitry on the same wafer, a capability that reduces system-level integration cost for customers building inertial measurement units, pressure sensors, and microphone arrays destined for defence platform integration.

Mixed-signal CMOS, spanning the 90nm-equivalent through mature nodes where SkyWater's process qualified, has served power management IC designers, precision analogue customers, and industrial interface chipmakers for whom the economics of a specialty-foundry relationship are preferable to competing for capacity allocation at a high-volume logic foundry running advanced-node processes at utilisation rates that leave little scheduling flexibility for low-volume production turns.

## Florida Center of Neovation: Advanced Packaging and the Next Conversion Layer

The Florida Center of Neovation (CoN), leased from Osceola County in Kissimmee and scaled through 2024 and 2025 with ~~CHIPS Act funding support~~ ==Florida state economic development and DoD-directed funding support==, added a ~~second~~ ==third== geographic node to SkyWater's manufacturing footprint ==alongside the Bloomington fab and the Fab 25/SkyWater Texas operation that has since wound down== and extended the company's capability set into advanced packaging — a segment whose strategic importance to the DoD has grown substantially as heterogeneous integration, chiplets, and 2.5D/3D assembly have become central to next-generation defence electronics architectures.

The CoN's advanced packaging capability addresses a gap that had previously required US defence programme managers to route die assembly and integration through offshore subcontractors, introducing supply-chain risk that the CHIPS Act's domestic-capacity provisions were explicitly designed to close. SkyWater's positioning at the CoN — offering packaging services that can receive die fabricated at the Bloomington trusted foundry and complete the assembly process under the same security posture — provides an end-to-end domestic manufacturing path for programmes requiring full chain-of-custody from wafer start through packaged device.

Commercial customers at the CoN have spanned the same specialty-process segments as the Bloomington wafer customer base, with the additional draw of integrated front-end and back-end services that reduce programme management complexity for fabless customers managing multi-vendor supply chains. ~~CHIPS Act funding~~ ==Florida EDA and DoD-directed funding== offsets reduced the capital cost burden of CoN equipment installation and qualification, accelerating the facility's readiness timeline relative to what a purely commercial financing structure would have supported. ==The CHIPS Act's direct preliminary memorandum of terms covering SkyWater capacity was issued for the Bloomington site rather than for the Florida facility.==

## Manufacturing Footprint Consolidated

| Facility | Location | Process Capability | Primary Customer Segments |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bloomington fab | Bloomington, MN | 200mm CMOS, RF SOI, MEMS, mixed-signal, superconducting | DoD Trusted Foundry, DARPA/IARPA, defence primes, specialty commercial |
| Center of Neovation | Kissimmee, FL | Advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration, 2.5D/3D assembly | DoD packaging programmes, commercial fabless customers |
| ==Fab 25 / SkyWater Texas== | ==Round Rock, TX== | ==200mm specialty CMOS (legacy)== | ==Wound down and reported as a discontinued facility/segment before the May 23, 2026 snapshot== |

Together the ~~two~~ ==two remaining== sites constitute the only US-owned, vertically integrated specialty foundry offering both front-end wafer fabrication under Trusted Foundry designation and advanced packaging under the same domestic-security umbrella — a structural position that CHIPS Act policy deliberately sought to incentivise, and that SkyWater entered the 2026 fiscal year positioned to monetise as defence electronics procurement shifted toward mandated domestic sourcing requirements.

chapters.title: Where SKYT sits against TSMC US fabs, GlobalFoundries Trusted Foundry, X-Fab specialty foundry, and broader foundry peers
chapters.body:
## A Moat Defined by Ownership, Not Just Accreditation

The semiconductor foundry landscape in 2025 sorted into three loose tiers relevant to the U.S. defense-industrial base: volume leaders with leading-edge nodes such as TSMC, Samsung, and Intel Foundry; specialty analog and mixed-signal houses serving automotive, industrial, and medical markets; and a narrow stratum of DMEA-accredited Trusted Foundries whose Category 1A status authorized them to touch classified microelectronics programs. SkyWater Technology occupied an intersection of the second and third tiers that no other company could replicate without years of capital investment and government vetting — the only pure-play foundry simultaneously 100% U.S.-owned, Category 1A accredited at both a front-end wafer fabrication facility and an advanced packaging site, and commercially active in superconducting electronics for quantum computing.

Thomas Sonderman framed the ownership question bluntly in late 2025:

> "We don't really have a foundry industry in the U.S. We have pockets of it, but other solutions just don't exist in the United States."

That absence was SkyWater's market.

## GlobalFoundries: The Scaled Rival With a Sovereign Caveat

The closest true peer in the Trusted Foundry category was GlobalFoundries. GF's Malta, New York Fab 8 received DMEA Category 1A accreditation in May 2023 — the same highest tier SkyWater's Bloomington fab had held since its recertification in March 2017. The September 2023 DoD award of a 10-year contract with a $3.1 billion ceiling — described by GF as "the third sequential 10-year contract of its kind" — underlined the depth of that government relationship. A separate $117 million agreement for strategic 45nm SOI supply established GF's mature-node defense lane explicitly alongside the longer frame agreement.

On revenue, the gap was stark. GlobalFoundries reported $6.79 billion in FY2025 against SkyWater's $442 million, a roughly 15-to-1 ratio. GF's Malta fab ran on 300mm wafers with processes reaching 12nm FinFET, while SkyWater's Minnesota facility operated on 200mm wafers anchored at 90nm for its primary CMOS platform~~, with 65nm available following the June 2025 acquisition of Infineon's Austin Fab 25~~ ==; the Austin Fab 25 site acquired from Infineon in June 2025 had since been wound down and disclosed as a closed facility ahead of the May 23, 2026 snapshot, leaving Bloomington and the Florida packaging site as the active footprint==.

Yet the ownership structure introduced a structural nuance. GlobalFoundries was majority-controlled by Mubadala Investment Company, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund. For contracts requiring Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence assessment — FOCI — that parentage complicated the path to classified programs in ways that 100% U.S.-owned SkyWater did not face. GF's CHIPS Act allocation of $1.5 billion dwarfed SkyWater's $16 million Bloomington, Minnesota award, but both carried National Security Guardrails; the guardrails applied differently when the ultimate beneficial owner was a foreign government entity. GF also disclosed no commercial superconducting or quantum foundry offering as of the snapshot date, and its defense revenue was subsumed within IoT and Communications categories on public filings, making direct comparison with SkyWater's disclosed defense-dominant ATS mix impractical.

## TSMC Arizona: Scale Without the Badge

TSMC's Arizona operation commanded the most attention in Washington and carried the largest CHIPS Act allocation at $6.6 billion finalized in April 2024, with a further $100 billion in domestic investment pledged in April 2025. Fab 1 in Phoenix entered high-volume N4/N5 production in the fourth quarter of 2024. Two additional Arizona fabs targeting N3 and N2/A16 process nodes were under construction through 2025 and into the following year.

The structural limitation was statutory rather than technical. TSMC Arizona LLC was a wholly owned subsidiary of a Taiwan Stock Exchange-listed company in which the Taiwan government retained a direct equity stake. That foreign ownership created FOCI exposure that, by Defense Department regulation, precluded DMEA Category 1A accreditation for classified microelectronics work. No Trusted Foundry designation had been reported for any TSMC Arizona facility as of the frozen snapshot date. The company's Arizona production was commercially oriented toward artificial intelligence accelerators, advanced mobile, and automotive chips — not the legacy defense program nodes on which long-lifecycle weapons systems depended. For a program office requiring classified ROIC production or rad-hard processing on 90nm infrastructure, TSMC Arizona offered nothing directly substitutable, regardless of its leading-edge commercial capability.

Sonderman recognized this dynamic when he observed in 2023 that "IP protection has become more important than low cost for many applications" and that customers "will pay a premium for supply chain certainty." TSMC Arizona represented the inverse of that calculus: extraordinary scale in service of leading-edge commercial performance, with classified defense work formally out of scope.

## Tower Semiconductor / JSTF: Defense Overlap, Different Specialty Stack

Tower Semiconductor's Newport Beach, California subsidiary — Jazz Semiconductor Trusted Foundry, or JSTF — carried both DMEA Category 1A and Category 1B accreditation, the latter adding scope for additional classified engagements. Accreditation dated to 2013 and 2014 respectively, predating SkyWater's current corporate structure. JSTF's process portfolio emphasized SiGe BiCMOS for millimeter-wave radar, RF CMOS from 65nm to 45nm, and CMOS image sensors — specialized capabilities that were complementary to rather than directly competitive with SkyWater's 90nm-anchored CMOS, MEMS, and superconducting platforms. Tower's FY2024 revenue of $1.44 billion placed it roughly three times SkyWater's scale for the same period, with no discrete defense segment reported publicly. A May 2026 partnership with Axiro Semiconductor to supply SiGe beamforming radar ICs illustrated the depth of Tower's analog millimeter-wave lane — terrain SkyWater did not contest.

One structural caveat applied: Tower's parent was Israel-headquartered, introducing its own FOCI considerations for U.S. classified programs, though JSTF's long-standing DoD accreditation demonstrated that a U.S.-subsidiary structure could satisfy the threshold under appropriate mitigation agreements.

## X-Fab: Commercial Specialty Without the Defense Ticket

X-Fab, listed on Euronext Paris with $816 million in FY2024 revenue, operated a six-fab network spanning Europe, Malaysia, and a Lubbock, Texas silicon carbide facility. Its specialty lay in analog and mixed-signal CMOS, SiC power devices, MEMS, and BCD processes for automotive, industrial, and medical markets. No DMEA Trusted Foundry designation had been reported. The Lubbock fab received a proposed $50 million CHIPS Act direct funding allocation in December 2024 — announced in the same batch as SkyWater's $16 million Bloomington, Minnesota award — but the capital was directed at SiC automotive production, not defense electronics. X-Fab and SkyWater overlapped in commercial MEMS and mixed-signal analog work, markets where process customization commanded premium margins, yet the defense lane was structurally inaccessible to X-Fab and the ATS co-development model that embedded SkyWater into customer process IP from early research through production was not an offering X-Fab publicly replicated.

## Intel Foundry Services: The Leading-Edge Defense Lane

Intel Foundry Services occupied a separate stratum. The Secure Enclave program, awarded up to $3 billion in CHIPS Act funding in September 2024, targeted leading-edge node manufacturing for U.S. government applications. Intel's 18A process — a 1.8nm-class node with PowerVia backside power delivery and RibbonFET gate-all-around transistors — positioned IFS as the domestic supplier for next-generation defense compute. The RAMP-C program brought Boeing and Northrop Grumman in as pilot customers through its Phase 2 and Phase 3 cycles, and the USMAG Alliance established a trusted design ecosystem for classified chip development on advanced nodes.

The node difference resolved the apparent overlap with SkyWater. Defense programs requiring bleeding-edge digital logic — advanced signal processing, AI inference at the edge, next-generation radar compute — looked to Intel IFS. Programs requiring sustained production of 90nm rad-hard processors, infrared readout ICs, mixed-signal sensors, and cryogenic electronics for quantum systems looked to SkyWater. The two companies were, in practice, suppliers to different acquisition programs within the same DoD budget.

## The Structural Comparison

| | SkyWater (SKYT) | GlobalFoundries (GFS) | TSMC Arizona | Tower / JSTF (TSEM) | X-Fab | Intel IFS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Latest FY revenue | $442M (FY2025) | $6.79B (FY2025) | N/A (subsidiary) | $1.44B (FY2024) | $816M (FY2024) | ~$4.4B |
| Primary wafer size | 200mm | 300mm | 300mm | 200mm | 200mm | 300mm |
| Finest defense-relevant node | ~~65nm (TX) / 90nm (MN)~~ ==90nm (MN); Austin TX site closed pre-snapshot== | 45nm SOI | None (no Trusted status) | 45nm RF CMOS | 180nm+ analog | 18A |
| DMEA Trusted status | Cat. 1A — MN fab + FL packaging | Cat. 1A — Malta NY | None | Cat. 1A + 1B — JSTF Newport Beach | None | Yes (historical) |
| U.S. ownership, no FOCI | ✓ 100% U.S. | ✗ UAE (Mubadala) | ✗ Taiwan-owned | ✗ Israel-headquartered | ✗ Belgian | ✓ U.S. (Intel Corp.) |
| Superconducting / quantum | ✓ 8 active programs (FY2025) | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| CHIPS Act allocation | $16M (MN fab) | $1.5B | $6.6B | Not disclosed | $50M (SiC TX) | $7.86B |

## Where the Moat Holds — and Where It Narrows

SkyWater's competitive position as of the frozen snapshot rested on three structural elements that peers could not quickly replicate: sole U.S. ownership with no FOCI exposure, DMEA Category 1A coverage across both front-end wafer fabrication and advanced packaging, and an active commercial superconducting qubit foundry capability that no other Trusted Foundry peer had established. That last element carried particular weight as quantum hardware scaled. D-Wave's March 2025 peer-reviewed demonstration of quantum supremacy in magnetic simulation — powered by SkyWater-fabricated qubits — was not an abstract proof-of-concept but a production validation milestone that GF, Tower, and Intel IFS could not cite.

The moat narrowed where process technology maturity intersected with program mix. GF's 45nm SOI defense platform was a full node generation ahead of SkyWater's 90nm CMOS in raw transistor density; Intel IFS's 18A was in a different universe entirely. For programs where leading-edge performance was the primary selection criterion and where FOCI mitigation could be structured at the subsidiary level, SkyWater was not the natural choice. The company's answer was to extend into domains where no Trusted Foundry peer was positioned: superconducting electronics for cryogenic quantum systems, fan-out wafer-level packaging through the Florida Center of Neovation, and the ATS co-development model that embedded SkyWater in customer process IP from earliest research through volume production.

> "AI has soared because TSMC is the foundry for the top AI design companies. That's essentially what we're doing here with quantum in the U.S."

That framing captured both the ambition and the constraint. TSMC reached scale through decades of commercial volume accumulation across thousands of customers. SkyWater's quantum and superconducting revenue remained a growth segment within an ATS mix still dominated by rad-hard, MEMS, and mixed-signal defense programs — quantum grew more than 30% in FY2025 but advanced compute as a whole accounted for only 15% of revenues by year-end. The structural moat was real and defensible; the question of whether it could anchor a revenue trajectory commensurate with the surrounding foundry landscape remained the central execution challenge through 2026 and the IonQ integration that followed.

chapters.title: Timeline from 2017 spin-out through 2021 IPO and CHIPS Act-supported scaling
chapters.body:
## The Oxbow Wager, 2017

When Oxbow Industries closed on its acquisition of Cypress Semiconductor's Bloomington, Minnesota fabrication plant in March 2017, the transaction registered barely a footnote in the semiconductor trade press. Cypress was tidying its balance sheet ahead of its eventual merger with Infineon; the 200mm fab — an 800,000-square-foot facility employing hundreds of workers in the Minneapolis exurbs — was an asset with a long operational history but no obvious strategic future inside the combined entity. What Oxbow recognized, and Cypress's corporate parent did not, was that Bloomington's combination of US ownership, operational maturity, and specialty process depth placed it at a structural intersection of three rising government priorities: domestic semiconductor capacity, defense supply-chain sovereignty, and advanced microelectronics research that no offshore foundry could service under ITAR constraints.

Thomas Sonderman, who assumed the chief executive title at the rebranded SkyWater Technology from the first day of the spin-out, had spent two decades inside semiconductor process development, including senior roles at AMD and GlobalFoundries. He understood that the commercial foundry race — driven by leading-edge lithography, measured in angstroms, and effectively monopolized by TSMC and Samsung — was not a contest SkyWater could or should enter. The defensible ground lay in specialty processes: silicon-on-insulator architectures suited to radio-frequency applications, microelectromechanical systems, mixed-signal CMOS, and superconducting electronics that cryogenic computing programs at DARPA required. Bloomington could serve customers who needed US-soil manufacturing, trusted supply chains, and process co-development flexibility — a market that commercial wafer price competition could not easily commoditize.

## Building the ATS-to-Wafer Flywheel

SkyWater's revenue architecture reflected that positioning from the outset. The company organized its commercial offering around two segments: Advanced Technology Services, under which engineers co-developed proprietary processes with customers and government research agencies; and Wafer Services, under which those developed processes were run at production volume for fabless customers and defense primes. The conceptual logic was a flywheel — ATS engagements would mature into Wafer Services production on an 18-to-36-month conversion lag — but in practice that lag created persistent revenue lumpiness during the pre-IPO growth years. DoD program timing, which operated on government budget cycles rather than commercial demand signals, amplified the quarterly variability.

Between 2017 and 2020, SkyWater accumulated Trusted Foundry designations from the Defense Microelectronics Activity and deepened engagements with Northrop Grumman, RTX-affiliated programs, and Lockheed Martin-connected suppliers that required ITAR-controlled, US-soil production. DARPA funded process development in superconducting electronics — a capability with almost no commercial analogue and therefore no foreign-foundry alternative — and IARPA research customers brought compound semiconductor work that reinforced the specialty moat. None of this progress was easily legible on a quarterly revenue basis. By the eve of the IPO, however, SkyWater had assembled a customer pipeline whose depth was unusual for a company of its revenue scale ~~==— FY2020 net sales of $140.4 million, up modestly from $136.7 million in FY2019==.

## The April 2021 NASDAQ Listing

SkyWater Technology priced its initial public offering on the NASDAQ Global Select Market in April 2021, listing under the ticker SKYT. The [S-1 registration statement](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=SKYT&type=S-1) documented a company whose revenue mix remained heavily weighted toward ATS — the higher-margin, lower-volume development work — and whose path to operating profitability was tied explicitly to ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion and utilization growth at Bloomington. The offering ~~raised capital intended in part to fund the early stages of what would become the Florida Center of Neovation, and it~~ placed Oxbow's long-term thesis in front of equity markets that, in the post-pandemic semiconductor shortage cycle of 2021, were unusually receptive to US-domestic capacity narratives ==— with Oxbow and affiliates retaining roughly 71.7% of the 39,059,743 shares outstanding after the full over-allotment, a controlling stake that preserved the original sponsor's strategic alignment well past the listing==.

The IPO timing was propitious but the execution path remained genuinely demanding. Converting ATS pipeline into Wafer Services production requires customers to complete process qualification, achieve yield targets, and commit to volume purchase agreements — a sequence that admits delays at every stage. SkyWater's revenue trajectory through 2022 and 2023 reflected that reality: DoD program timing created quarter-to-quarter variability, Wafer Services growth lagged ATS revenue accumulation, and operating losses persisted, funded through equity raises that diluted the post-IPO shareholder base but preserved the capital structure needed to pursue the Florida expansion.

## Florida Center of Neovation

The Florida Center of Neovation — located in Kissimmee under a lease arrangement with Osceola County — represented SkyWater's most capital-intensive strategic commitment after the IPO. The facility was designed not as a second full-service fab in the Bloomington mold, but as an advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration hub, capturing rising demand for chiplet assembly, interposer technology, and system-level integration work that defense and commercial customers increasingly required alongside wafer fabrication. The Osceola County lease structure transferred meaningful construction-cost exposure to the public-sector partner, reducing SkyWater's upfront capital requirement while committing the company to a multi-year Florida operating footprint.

Sonderman framed the Florida CoN as a capability extension rather than a narrow capacity expansion: where Bloomington provided the specialty wafer processes, Kissimmee would supply the assembly and integration layer that converted individual die into deployable system components. For DoD customers in particular, having both layers under US-soil, US-owned control, and within a single trusted supply chain represented a differentiator that no domestic competitor could fully replicate at comparable specialty-process depth through the 2024–2025 scaling window. ==The third leg of SkyWater's footprint — Fab 25 in Austin, Texas, acquired from Infineon — was wound down and reported as a closed facility ahead of the May 2026 snapshot, leaving Bloomington and Kissimmee as the operating sites at the dossier date.==

## ~~CHIPS Act~~ ==Federal and State== Alignment and Forward Catalysts

The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 defined the federal funding architecture that SkyWater moved to access across 2024 and 2025 ==for its Bloomington fab==. The Department of Commerce's CHIPS Program Office ~~announced support for both the Florida Center of Neovation expansion and Bloomington fab modernization during that window~~ ==signed a Preliminary Memorandum of Terms in support of Bloomington fab modernization during that window, while the Florida Center of Neovation drew on a distinct funding mix routed through Department of Defense microelectronics programs and Florida state economic-development channels rather than a direct CHIPS Act award==, formalizing a relationship between the company's capital plan and the federal government's domestic semiconductor agenda that had been implicit since the 2017 spin-out. CHIPS Act funding, as structured, offsets a fraction of eligible capital expenditures rather than fully underwriting expansion — SkyWater remained responsible for matching investment and sustained operational execution.

The strategic logic was mutually reinforcing: ==the Bloomington== CHIPS Program Office ~~awards~~ ==PMT== validated the defense and government research customer base that had anchored the ATS pipeline since 2017, while the Trusted Foundry production history gave the program office a de-risked operational track record uncommon among applicants. Final disbursement amounts for the ~~Florida CoN tranche~~ ==Bloomington CHIPS tranche, and milestone-linked draws on the Florida CoN's DoD and state EDA support,== remained subject to program ~~office~~ milestones through the frozen-snapshot date of May 2026, and the pace of Wafer Services revenue conversion from the current ATS cohort — specifically the tape-out milestones that trigger volume purchase commitments — remained the central inflection point for Bloomington utilization and operating leverage. Additional DoD program wins in superconducting electronics and RF SOI, and incremental DARPA and IARPA awards, represented upside optionality against a baseline capital program ~~already underwritten by the public-private CHIPS structure ==anchored by the Bloomington CHIPS PMT and the Florida DoD/state EDA package==. What began as a quiet Midwest foundry acquisition in 2017 had, by the middle of the decade, become a test case for whether US industrial policy could convert defense microelectronics dependency into durable domestic capacity.

chapters.title: Process technology IP, DoD security accreditations, Bloomington and Florida engineering
chapters.body:
SkyWater Technology built its competitive position not on silicon volume but on the depth and defensibility of its specialty process intellectual property. Where the large foundries competed on node shrinks and wafer-out capacity, SkyWater accumulated a library of differentiated process families—each requiring distinct materials engineering, tooling configurations, and government qualification regimes—that were impractical for commodity fabs to replicate and legally impossible for offshore foundries to access in classified applications. That IP breadth, developed at the Bloomington site across the Cypress Semiconductor years and extended through government co-development agreements after the 2017 spin-out, formed the engine of the Advanced Technology Services model and the strategic rationale behind successive rounds of federal investment.

## A Portfolio Built on Specialty Nodes

SkyWater's [process technology offering](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/mems-photonics-and-custom/) drew from nine distinct technology families across the frozen window. The mixed-signal CMOS platforms at 90 nanometers and 130 nanometers served readout integrated circuits, sensor front-ends, and analog-intensive designs where density mattered less than noise performance and reliability qualification. A radio-frequency silicon-on-insulator capability addressed the low-loss switching and high-frequency requirements of defense communications and radar payloads.

The microelectromechanical systems portfolio spanned the full transducer architecture range: capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducers, pressure sensors, microbolometers for infrared detection, resonators, biosensors, and microfluidic devices. The breadth reflected more than a decade of customer-specific co-development at Bloomington. Integrated photonics operated at 55nm-capable single-patterning lithography, supporting high-aspect-ratio waveguides, grating couplers, optical modulators, and diffraction gratings with pitches down to 0.28 micrometers—a resolution unusual for a 200mm production environment. Carbon nanotube field-effect transistor integration, pursued with academic and government research partners, anchored the frontier edge of the portfolio and remained in the co-development phase through the frozen window.

The company maintained AS9100 aerospace, ISO 9001, IATF 16949 automotive, and ISO 13485 medical device certifications across its platforms—a qualification matrix that reflected the regulatory diversity of its customer base and imposed meaningful barriers to competitive entry.

## DoD Trusted Foundry: Dual-Site Accreditation

The security architecture underpinning SkyWater's defense business rested on Defense Microelectronics Activity Category 1A Trusted Foundry accreditation—the highest designation available to a commercial semiconductor manufacturer. The [Bloomington fab received Cat1A on March 20, 2017](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-technology-foundry-achieves-cat1a-trusted-foundry-accreditation-from-u-s-department-of-defense/), accomplished within two weeks of the Oxbow Industries acquisition from Cypress. The speed was not incidental: the site had operated under controlled-access DoD production regimes for years under Cypress, and the transition preserved the physical security infrastructure, personnel vetting systems, and design-to-fab information controls that DMEA auditors required. The accreditation authorized SkyWater to provide wafer fabrication, design services, wafer testing, and brokerage to defense customers under DoD Instruction 5200.44, which mandated trusted domestic sourcing for mission-critical custom microelectronics.

The [Florida Center of Neovation achieved DMEA Category 1A Trusted Supplier accreditation on May 14, 2024](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-florida-achieves-dmea-category-1a-trusted-supplier-accreditation/), specifically covering its fan-out wafer-level packaging capabilities. The extension of Cat1A to Florida completed a fully Trusted-accredited manufacturing chain from front-end wafer processing in Minnesota through back-end advanced packaging in Florida—closing a gap that had previously forced defense primes to accept non-Trusted packaging steps outside the continental United States.

## The Radiation-Hardened Build-Out

SkyWater's most capital-intensive technology development program of the period was the radiation-hardened process build-out at Bloomington. The Department of Defense committed [up to $170 million across multiple phases](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/us-department-of-defense-to-invest-up-to-170m-at-skywater-for-rad-hard-technology/) to develop a production-ready 90nm rad-hard by process fully depleted silicon-on-insulator platform—designated RH90—derived from process technology developed at MIT Lincoln Laboratory and adapted for commercial 200mm production. Phase one carried an $80 million initial funding commitment covering up to 15,000 square feet of new cleanroom area and copper dual-damascene interconnect integration, which offered lower resistance and higher interconnect density than the aluminum baseline.

A July 2022 [Other Transactional Agreement option of $27 million](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/us-department-of-defense-awards-skywater-a-27m-option-to-facilitate-american-made-semiconductors-critical-to-national-security-and-domestic-supply-chains/) then funded the IP ecosystem built around RH90—process design kit development, IP library qualification through Trusted Semiconductor Solutions, multi-project wafer shuttle launches, and radiation and reliability testing managed by CAES. Sonderman framed the company's posture: "As a U.S.-based and operated pure-play semiconductor foundry, we are committed to our role in reshoring chip manufacturing."

## Florida Center of Neovation: Advanced Packaging

SkyWater Florida's [Center of Neovation](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-expanding-with-florida-facility-to-accelerate-domestic-advanced-packaging-capabilities-for-microelectronics-manufacturing/)—a 109,000-square-foot facility with approximately 36,000 square feet of cleanroom space leased from Osceola County inside the Neocity technology district in Kissimmee—concentrated on fan-out wafer-level packaging and heterogeneous integration, capabilities largely absent from U.S. domestic production before SkyWater's 2021 entry.

Federal support arrived through two channels. A [$36.5 million Department of Commerce grant](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-to-leverage-36-5m-department-of-commerce-grant-to-the-florida-semiconductor-coalition-to-expand-its-advanced-packaging-facility-operations-in-florida/) channeled through the Florida Semiconductor Coalition funded cleanroom expansion and tooling. Separately, a five-year DoD contract under the RESHAPE (Re-shore Ecosystem for Secure Heterogeneous Advanced Packaged Electronics) program, awarded jointly with Deca Technologies, carried a [$120 million base value with options to $190 million](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywater-florida-and-deca-technologies-announce-120m-dod-award-to-expand-advanced-packaging-capabilities-in-osceola-county-florida/) and directly addressed Pentagon concerns about advanced packaging concentration in Taiwan and South Korea.

## Superconducting Electronics and the Quantum Edge

SkyWater's superconducting electronics practice—200mm process integration for low-temperature Josephson Junction devices across six or more metal layers—dated its commercial origins to 2013 at Bloomington. That decade-long investment, sustained in part through DARPA-funded programs and served by SkyWater's Trusted Foundry security posture, positioned the company as the principal domestic contract manufacturer for superconducting qubit and cryogenic control electronics development.

The practice's most visible external validation arrived in [March 2025](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/skywaters-commercially-fabricated-qubits-power-d-waves-landmark-achievement-in-quantum-supremacy/), when D-Wave published a peer-reviewed paper in *Science* demonstrating that its Advantage2 annealing quantum computer—whose qubits were fabricated entirely at Bloomington using SkyWater's custom material deposition and specialized device patterning—had outperformed one of the world's most powerful classical supercomputers in magnetic materials simulation. "SkyWater is proud of our longstanding partnership with D-Wave and this unprecedented innovation in quantum computing," Sonderman said at the announcement, pointing to the broader necessity of expanding U.S. semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure for advanced quantum hardware. The ten-year fabrication relationship had produced a commercially manufactured device capable of beyond-classical performance—a commercial proof-point that reinforced the strategic logic behind IonQ's January 2026 agreement to [acquire SkyWater at an implied equity value of approximately $1.8 billion](https://www.skywatertechnology.com/ionq-to-acquire-skywater/), ~~pending regulatory and shareholder approvals~~ ==with SkyWater stockholders having approved the transaction on May 8, 2026 and the deal pending remaining regulatory clearances==.

chapters.title: ATS conversion timing, Florida execution, DoD program timing, Oxbow governance, dilution, competitive
chapters.body:
## The Conversion Clock

No variable carried more weight in the SkyWater Technology investment thesis than the lag between Advanced Technology Services revenue and the Wafer Services production volume that followed it. ATS work — process development engineering, mask iterations, prototype runs — arrived as recognizable revenue first, typically contracted with a single customer or government program and executed across quarters. The payoff came later, when a customer's process cleared qualification and committed to production volume. That interval ranged, by SkyWater's own characterisation in successive annual filings, from eighteen months to three years or more depending on process complexity, customer readiness, and yield milestones.

The risk embedded in that structure was straightforward but underappreciated by early investors: any ATS engagement that slowed, stalled, or failed to qualify did not convert. Revenue recognised during the development phase became a sunk cost for the customer and a gap in SkyWater's Wafer Services backlog. Because the company ran a concentrated customer roster — defense primes, government agencies, and a small number of specialty commercial accounts — the failure of even one major program to reach production could produce a perceptible revenue step-down twelve to eighteen months forward. SkyWater's Wafer Services revenue as a share of total revenue remained lower than management had originally guided at the time of the April 2021 IPO, reflecting the serial nature of qualification cycles and the difficulty of compressing them.

Thomas Sonderman acknowledged the dynamic directly in multiple earnings calls, characterising the pipeline as inherently "lumpy" — a word that appeared across quarters as a structural admission rather than an excuse. The absence of a large-volume commodity customer meant that each conversion event mattered individually, and that the aggregate conversion rate in any given year was as much a function of external customer decisions as of SkyWater's own execution.

## Florida: Capital Before Revenue

The Florida Center of Neovation introduced a second, distinct execution risk layered atop the ATS conversion dynamic. The facility in Kissimmee — leased from Osceola County, Florida on terms that reduced SkyWater's initial capital outlay but embedded long-term occupancy obligations — was designed to house advanced packaging capabilities that neither the Bloomington fab nor most US foundries offered at meaningful scale. The strategic logic was sound: advanced packaging had become a differentiating capability as semiconductor customers sought chiplet integration and heterogeneous architectures, and DoD customers in particular wanted packaging performed inside a trusted, domestically controlled environment.

The operational risk, however, was the gap between capital deployment and revenue recognition. Equipping an advanced packaging facility required sustained capital expenditure — tooling, cleanroom buildout, process qualification — before a single wafer or package shipped commercially. ~~CHIPS Act funding announcements across 2024 and 2025 provided partial offsets, but CHIPS disbursements historically followed milestones rather than arriving as upfront grants, meaning SkyWater continued to absorb cash outflows on a lead-lag basis.~~ ==State of Florida, Osceola County, EDA and DoD program support announced across 2024 and 2025 provided partial offsets at the Florida site — the public CHIPS PMT covered the Bloomington, Minnesota fab rather than Florida — but those non-CHIPS Florida disbursements were similarly milestone-contingent rather than arriving as upfront grants, meaning SkyWater continued to absorb cash outflows on a lead-lag basis.== The Osceola County lease structure, while politically supportive and diplomatically valuable for landing state and federal backing, also constrained SkyWater's optionality: the facility needed to ramp to justify the long-term lease obligations, regardless of how quickly commercial demand materialised.

Hiring risk compounded the capital execution problem. Central Florida did not have an established semiconductor workforce comparable to what Minnesota's legacy of IBM and Cray and Control Data had seeded in the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro. Every skilled process engineer, equipment technician, and quality specialist at the CoN had to be recruited from out of state, trained on SkyWater's specific processes, or developed internally — all of which added time and cost that was difficult to model in advance.

## DoD: Sole-Source Visibility Is Not Certainty

DoD Trusted Foundry designation was SkyWater's most durable competitive moat: the company held one of the relatively few active US-owned fab qualifications enabling sole-source production of microelectronics for sensitive defense applications. The designation was not meaningfully threatened within the frozen window. But the timing and size of individual program awards remained volatile in ways that affected quarterly and annual revenue recognition substantially.

Defense procurement ran on Congressional appropriations cycles, continuing resolutions, and program-specific budget decisions that could delay wafer orders by quarters without any change in SkyWater's competitive position. A program that was "in development" in one fiscal year might receive production funding the next — or might sit through a continuing resolution with authorisation but not appropriation, leaving SkyWater holding capacity and incurring costs against revenue that had not yet been recognised. The company's defense-prime customers — Northrop Grumman, RTX, and Lockheed Martin-affiliated programs — were themselves subject to DoD procurement cycles, meaning SkyWater sat two links down from the ultimate budget decision. DARPA and IARPA research contracts added shorter-duration but similarly uncertain renewal profiles.

The resulting pattern was a revenue line that moved with program calendars rather than with any underlying demand weakness. Sonderman consistently characterised the DoD demand as structurally intact, but timing risk was real: a quarter in which two large program orders slipped could produce a meaningful miss against expectations without any deterioration in the underlying pipeline.

## Oxbow and the Governance Overhang

Oxbow Industries, the private investment vehicle that acquired the Cypress Semiconductor Bloomington fab in March 2017 and rebranded it SkyWater Technology, retained a controlling equity position well into the post-IPO period. The April 2021 NASDAQ listing reduced Oxbow's absolute ownership but left the firm with sufficient voting power to exert material influence over board composition, capital allocation, and strategic direction. SkyWater's S-1 and successive DEF 14A proxy filings disclosed the concentration of voting power and the related-party relationships that flowed from it.

The governance overhang created a structural tension familiar in founder-control or sponsor-control companies: minority public shareholders bore market risk while the controlling holder could shape decisions that did not require a shareholder vote. The board's composition — with Oxbow-affiliated directors holding seats through the frozen window — meant that capital allocation decisions, including decisions about when and how aggressively to raise additional equity, were made within a framework that reflected Oxbow's own return horizon and exit considerations as much as the preferences of the public float.

## Dilution as Operating Reality

SkyWater's decision to pursue the Florida Center of Neovation at meaningful scale, combined with operating losses during the extended ramp phase, produced a predictable consequence: repeated returns to equity markets. Post-IPO capital raises diluted existing shareholders in a pattern that was disclosed and anticipated but no less consequential. Each equity offering at prices below the IPO level compounded the dilution impact on early investors.

The CHIPS Act funding provided some relief — grant and loan program support ==for the Bloomington fab== reduced the pure-equity funding requirement — but CHIPS disbursements were milestone-contingent and slow to arrive. In the interim, equity remained the primary lever. Stock-based compensation to retain engineers and executives in a competitive talent market added a further layer of non-cash dilution that ran through the income statement and into share count each quarter. As of the frozen window, the fully-diluted share count had grown materially from the IPO baseline.

## Competitive Pressure: Scale Gap and Trusted Access

| Competitor | Trusted Foundry Status | Primary Advantage | Scale (wafer capacity) |
|---|---|---|---|
| GlobalFoundries | Yes (DMEA-qualified) | 300mm volume, >GF 14nm nodes, multi-fab redundancy | Substantially larger |
| TSMC US (Arizona) | In process | Sub-5nm capability; US-soil production | Substantially larger |
| X-Fab | Specialty processes | European-headquartered; specialty CMOS, SiC | Comparable specialty niche |
| SkyWater | Yes (DMEA-qualified) | Only pure-play US-owned specialty foundry | Smallest |

GlobalFoundries posed the most direct threat in the Trusted Foundry lane. Its DMEA qualification, US fabrication footprint across New York and Vermont, and far larger installed capacity gave it options on large-volume defense production that SkyWater could not match. For programs that required only trust designation and standard CMOS nodes, GlobalFoundries could compete on price and delivery in ways SkyWater could not undercut.

TSMC's Arizona expansion — supported by its own substantial CHIPS Act funding — raised the longer-term question of whether advanced-node capability on US soil would eventually commoditise the "domestic trusted production" premium that SkyWater had relied upon. TSMC Arizona remained focused on leading-edge nodes rather than specialty processes, but its presence signalled that the US government's willingness to fund domestic capacity would eventually produce a more competitive landscape, even if the timelines extended well beyond the frozen window.

SkyWater's defensible position rested on process specialisation — superconducting electronics, RF SOI, MEMS, mixed-signal CMOS — that the large-volume foundries neither prioritised nor were optimised to develop. The risk was not displacement so much as commoditisation of the trust premium over time, and the possibility that a well-capitalised competitor could choose to enter the specialty DoD segment deliberately if the market grew large enough to justify the investment.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Earnings Calendar: Twelve Months From the Snapshot

At the frozen-snapshot date of 23 May 2026, SkyWater Technology has just cleared the Q1 2026 earnings cycle — results typically reported in late April or early May — and sits roughly three months ahead of Q2 2026 disclosures. ==The forward calendar below assumes SkyWater operates as a standalone reporting company; SkyWater stockholders in fact approved the IonQ merger at $35.00 per SkyWater share on 8 May 2026, so the events outlined apply only in the contingency that the transaction does not close before each report date.== Four earnings events are visible on the forward horizon before the snapshot window closes in May 2027: Q2 2026, Q3 2026, the full-year 2026 annual results, and Q1 2027. Each carries distinct thesis-testing weight that investors should calendar in advance.

**Q2 2026 (expected late July or early August 2026)** is the first material read on whether Florida Center of Neovation production throughput has accelerated since Q1 commentary. The central question is whether advanced packaging tool utilisation has crossed the threshold at which customer qualification programs — initiated in late 2025 — have converted to billable Wafer Services volume. Any explicit revenue attribution to Florida that Sonderman or the CFO team calls out in prepared remarks or Q&A would constitute meaningful forward signal. In prior quarters, Sonderman has drawn direct lines between named customer design-win qualifications and anticipated facility ramp timelines; investors should watch for that language to shift from conditional to confirmatory.

**Q3 2026 (expected late October or early November 2026)** is the critical DoD visibility quarter. The federal government's fiscal year turns on 30 September; new programme appropriations, contract awards, and Trusted Foundry production orders flow through the October-November window. Historically, Q3 SkyWater results have carried the highest probability of new DoD programme announcements or Advanced Technology Services contract extensions — events that function as leading indicators for Wafer Services conversion 18 to 36 months hence.

**Q4 2026 and the full-year report (expected February or March 2027)** will provide the first clean look at whether the operating leverage thesis — that revenue growth above a certain threshold generates disproportionate margin improvement as the Bloomington 200mm fab approaches higher utilisation — has begun appearing in the income statement. Management guidance for FY2027, issued on this call, is likely to be the single most consequential near-term investor event across the entire 12-month window ==absent the IonQ deal closing first==.

---

## Consensus Estimates and the Growth Trajectory

Sell-side consensus as of the frozen snapshot — calibrated to Q1 2026 actuals ==of $160.7 million== and most recent management commentary — positions SkyWater on the following forward trajectory. Coverage remains thin, typically four to six active models, meaning the consensus band is wide and individual estimates diverge materially on the Florida CoN contribution assumption.

| Period | Revenue (consensus midpoint) | YoY growth implied | Adj. operating result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026 | ~~$82–92M~~ ==~$160–175M== | ~~10–15%~~ ==~45–55%== | Negative; sequential improvement |
| Q3 2026 | ~~$87–100M~~ ==~$165–180M== | ~~12–18%~~ ==~45–55%== | Narrow operating loss |
| Q4 2026 | ~~$88–105M~~ ==~$170–190M== | ~~10–18%~~ ==~40–55%== | Near break-even on adjusted basis |
| FY2026 | ~~$345–385M~~ ==~$655–705M== | ~~10–15% vs FY2025E~~ ==~48–60% vs FY2025 actual== | Adj. EBITDA positive; GAAP loss narrowing |

The implied FY2026 range of ~~$345–385M~~ ==$655–705M== would represent a step-up from ~~the $300–320M baseline expectation for FY2025~~ ==FY2025 actual revenue of $442.1 million==, driven in roughly equal proportion by Florida advanced packaging revenue recognition and continued ATS-to-Wafer-Services conversion at Bloomington. GAAP earnings per share are expected to remain negative through at least H1 2027. The profitability debate centres on whether operating leverage turns sharply enough in H2 2026 to produce a positive adjusted operating result — an outcome that would almost certainly trigger a material multiple re-rating in any standalone scenario ~~, given the stock's persistent infrastructure-discount valuation~~ ==, though with SKYT now trading against the fixed $35.00 IonQ exchange and an implied roughly $1.8 billion equity value, that re-rating channel has effectively been closed to current holders==.

---

## Management Guidance: Milestones Over Numbers

SkyWater does not provide traditional quarterly revenue guidance; rather, Sonderman and the CFO team have consistently framed forward expectations in terms of programme milestones and capacity inflection points. On the Q4 2025 earnings call, the characterisation was directional rather than numeric:

> "We expect 2026 to be a year where the investments we've made in Florida and the process development work we've done for multiple customers over the past two to three years starts to show up in production revenue. The funnel has never been larger."

That statement sets a high qualitative bar that the market will hold the company to across every quarterly print. Any slippage in Florida production ramp timing, or any commentary suggesting customer qualification schedules have pushed out, will be read as a miss against this implicit commitment regardless of whether revenue is technically within the guidance band.

The CHIPS Act deployment timeline adds a second layer of external milestones. ~~SkyWater's Florida CoN expansion has been supported by direct CHIPS Act disbursement alongside matching infrastructure investment from Osceola County.~~ ==The public CHIPS Preliminary Memorandum of Terms in fact covers SkyWater's Bloomington, Minnesota fab; the Florida CoN expansion has been backed by Florida economic-development incentives and Department of Defense funding alongside matching infrastructure investment from Osceola County.== Milestone-based funding tranches — contingent on verified capital deployment and employment targets — create checkpoints visible through Commerce Department disclosures and company 8-K filings. Investors should calendar any CHIPS Office milestone certification announcements ==tied to the Bloomington PMT== as independent third-party confirmation of ramp execution, separate from what management chooses to disclose voluntarily.

---

## What to Watch Each Quarter

**Q2 2026 scorecard.** Three metrics carry thesis weight. First, Florida CoN revenue as a percentage of quarterly total — any contribution above 8 to 10% of the quarterly print would represent a structural shift from the historically Bloomington-dominant mix. Second, an implied ATS book-to-bill proxy, typically inferrable from management commentary on backlog health even when not formally reported. Third, gross margin trajectory — any expansion above the mid-to-high-teens range signals that Bloomington utilisation is recovering and that Florida is contributing positive-margin Wafer Services volume rather than dilutive ATS development revenue.

**Q3 2026 scorecard.** Defence programme disclosure is the primary watch item. A new DoD Trusted Foundry production contract, a DARPA programme extension, or a named superconducting electronics programme milestone — DARPA's cryogenic and superconducting electronics work has been a recurring ATS category — would extend the forward DoD revenue visibility that underpins a significant portion of the bull thesis. Conversely, any commentary about programme delays or budget pressure on defence research appropriations warrants attention, particularly if the continuing-resolution pattern that characterised FY2025 federal spending recurs.

**Q4 2026 scorecard.** Operating leverage inflection is the definitive test. At the FY2026 revenue scale implied by consensus, SkyWater should be generating sufficient gross profit to absorb its fixed-cost base and begin narrowing the GAAP operating loss materially. If Q4 gross margin does not show meaningful sequential expansion from Q2 and Q3 levels, the profitability timeline shifts toward 2028 or later — a de-rating trigger that ~~would likely compress the multiple back toward trough historical levels~~ ==in a standalone scenario would compress the multiple back toward trough historical levels, though as a practical matter the IonQ exchange has already pinned the SKYT equity value at $35.00 per share==.

---

## The Bull and Bear Setup

**The bull case** rests on three compounding factors. The ATS-to-Wafer-Services pipeline assembled across 2023 through 2025 — spanning defence, commercial MEMS, specialty RF, and advanced packaging — is at a point in the conversion cycle where volume production authorisations should be materialising through 2026. The Florida CoN advanced packaging facility represents a revenue stream with essentially no legacy comparable, meaning early traction is incrementally additive rather than displacing Bloomington volume. And the ==Bloomington== CHIPS Act funding ==package==, ==combined with Florida EDA and DoD support for the CoN buildout,== reduces capital intensity burden on equity holders while providing a degree of government-sponsored demand visibility that no purely commercial foundry can claim.

In this scenario, FY2026 revenue breaks toward the high end of the ~~$345–385M~~ ==$655–705M== range, gross margins exit the year north of 20% for the first time in the company's public history, and Sonderman can credibly guide to GAAP operating profitability in 2027. ~~A re-rating from infrastructure-discount to growth-with-visibility would imply substantial upside from current levels.~~ ==Because SKYT now trades against the fixed $35.00 IonQ exchange, any such operational upside accrues to the post-close combined IonQ entity rather than to current SKYT holders.==

**The bear case** is a timing story rather than a structural one. SkyWater has faced customer qualification pushouts, DoD programme delays tied to Congressional appropriations timelines, and Florida construction or tooling setbacks that have shifted anticipated revenue into future quarters on more than one occasion since the IPO. If Q2 2026 reveals that Florida CoN revenue recognition is again below expectations — a major customer's qualification process extended from Q2 into Q4, for example — the market's patience with the ramp narrative will be tested. The bear scenario does not require any fundamental deterioration in the competitive position or the DoD Trusted Foundry franchise; it requires only that timing slippage continues to erode the credibility of forward guidance ==— a risk that, post-stockholder approval, matters chiefly insofar as severe operational disappointment could give IonQ grounds to renegotiate or walk==.

~~The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot tilts toward the bull case on a 12-to-18-month horizon, but with material quarterly-level volatility around each earnings event. Investors with exposure to SKYT are positioned not in a binary-outcome stock but in one with a sequenced series of thesis-validation gates — each clearable, none guaranteed — beginning with the Q2 2026 print in late July.~~ ==With SkyWater stockholders having approved the IonQ merger on 8 May 2026, the asymmetry at the frozen snapshot is governed less by the standalone earnings path than by the probability and timing of deal close. The quarterly gates above still matter — primarily for IonQ's pro-forma planning and for the residual risk that the transaction breaks — but SKYT holders are positioned in a spread to the $35.00 exchange rather than in a sequenced standalone thesis-validation trade, beginning with the Q2 2026 print in late July.==

chapters.title: ATS-to-Wafer conversion, Florida ramp, CHIPS Act deployment, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
The central wager at SkyWater Technology has always been temporal: spend years developing a customer's novel semiconductor process under an Advanced Technology Services contract, then reap volume Wafer Services revenue when that process reaches production. The gap between those two events — measured in company filings as eighteen to thirty-six months but routinely stretching longer for the most complex programmes — defined both the financial cadence and the investment thesis since Thomas Sonderman led the March 2017 spin-out from Cypress Semiconductor's Bloomington fab.

By early 2026, that wager was entering a phase of partial resolution. Several ATS programmes originating in 2022 and 2023 had reached or were approaching tape-out maturity. The Florida Center of Neovation in Kissimmee was transitioning from a construction-and-qualification story into an early-revenue story. And ~~two rounds of CHIPS Act support~~ ==the Bloomington CHIPS Act Preliminary Memorandum of Terms, together with separate state, EDA, and DoD facility funding behind the Florida Center of Neovation,== had begun displacing a portion of the capital burden that had kept the income statement in deficit since the April 2021 NASDAQ listing.

## The Conversion Flywheel

SkyWater reports two revenue lines: Advanced Technology Services, which captures engineering labour and non-recurring engineering fees as a customer's process is developed and qualified; and Wafer Services, which captures production volume once that process enters manufacturing. The ratio between them has historically understated the company's industrial progress, because ATS fees — though recognised as earned — represent future Wafer volume embedded in a pipeline invisible to the income statement.

The conversion dynamic operates across three distinct horizons. Near-term, incremental Wafer Services revenue accretes as processes completed in 2022–2024 cross qualification milestones and move to volume. Medium-term, the Florida Center of Neovation adds a second ==active== manufacturing node ==— following the wind-down of Fab 25/SkyWater Texas, which the company had previously reported as a separate facility and segment —== oriented toward advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration, and the compound-semiconductor adjacencies that defence and space customers increasingly specify. Long-term, the DoD Trusted Foundry designation anchors a recurring programme base that provides revenue visibility at a multi-year cadence few commercial foundry relationships can match.

Sonderman has consistently characterised the ATS pipeline as the leading indicator the market most frequently misreads. In this framework, an ATS quarter that appears flat or declining may simply reflect a cohort of programmes transitioning from development fees to wafer revenue — a shift that compresses the top-line numerator while expanding the production backlog. For investors conditioned to read sequential ATS softness as demand deterioration, the lag structure has been a persistent source of misvaluation and, periodically, a source of stock-price volatility that bore little relation to underlying programme progress.

## Florida Center of Neovation: The Second Manufacturing Node

The Florida Center of Neovation occupies a facility in Kissimmee leased from Osceola County under terms structured to align landlord incentives with fab utilisation — an arrangement that shifted a portion of facility carrying cost off SkyWater's balance sheet during the ramp phase. The facility's equipment base was scaled in tranches, with ~~CHIPS Act funding~~ ==Florida state, EDA, and DoD facility funding== partially offsetting tool procurement costs that would otherwise have required additional equity dilution from shareholders already carrying a multi-year paper loss since the IPO.

By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the CoN had completed initial equipment qualification in its advanced packaging lines and was supporting a customer mix weighted toward DoD-adjacent programmes and research-grade volumes. The facility's strategic importance extended beyond its near-term revenue contribution: it provided SkyWater with a geographically distributed manufacturing footprint — significant for business continuity and for US government customers whose supply-chain requirements increasingly specified geographic separation from single-site dependencies at Bloomington ==once the Texas footprint was retired==.

The CoN's packaging capabilities were complementary to, rather than duplicative of, Bloomington. Where Bloomington anchored the front-end process library — CMOS down to 90nm equivalent, RF SOI, MEMS, mixed-signal, superconducting electronics — Kissimmee extended SkyWater's offering into back-end heterogeneous integration: chiplet assembly, advanced packaging formats, and the module-level integration workflows that defence electronics customers required when sourcing from a Trusted Foundry that could close the manufacturing loop entirely within US territory.

## CHIPS Act Capital Deployment
