The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 identified domestic specialty foundry capacity as a programme priority alongside the high-profile leading-edge investments anchored by TSMC's Arizona fabs and Intel's CHIPS-backed expansion. SkyWater positioned itself within the specialty and mature-node tier and ~~received CHIPS Act support across both the Bloomington modernisation programme and the Florida CoN expansion~~ ==secured a public CHIPS Act Preliminary Memorandum of Terms for the Bloomington, Minnesota modernisation programme, while the Florida Center of Neovation expansion was backed by a separate package of Florida state, county, EDA, and DoD facility funding rather than a direct CHIPS Act award==. [SkyWater IR / CHIPS Act announcements, 2024–2025](https://ir.skywatertechnology.com)

The significance of ~~CHIPS Act funding~~ ==this federal and state capital stack== for SkyWater was structural rather than merely additive. At the company's scale — mid-size by global foundry standards, operating in a segment where customer programmes often required multi-year NRE investment before Wafer revenue materialised — the capital cost of maintaining and expanding a manufacturing platform had historically demanded equity raises that diluted existing shareholders. ~~CHIPS Act grants and incentives~~ ==The Bloomington CHIPS PMT, alongside the Florida EDA and DoD facility commitments,== shifted a portion of that cost to the federal balance sheet, improving the internal economics of programme wins that would otherwise have carried marginal return profiles during the extended ramp period.

Equally important was the demand-signal function ~~the CHIPS Act~~ ==these overlapping federal programmes== created. Federal investment in a domestic specialty foundry carried implicit endorsement for DoD programme offices, DARPA and IARPA programme managers, and defence prime contractors evaluating their supply-chain sovereignty requirements. SkyWater's ~~CHIPS Act designation~~ ==CHIPS PMT at Bloomington, combined with DoD-funded build-out in Florida,== reinforced a competitive moat that GlobalFoundries — the other principal US-based Trusted Foundry — competed against from a larger but less specialty-oriented platform.

## DoD Demand Visibility and the Defence Programme Base

SkyWater's DoD Trusted Foundry designation underpinned a recurring programme base since well before the CHIPS Act era. Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, and Lockheed Martin-affiliated programmes drew on Bloomington's process library for application-specific integrated circuits that required domestic-only manufacturing. DARPA's superconducting electronics programme — developing cryogenic processor architectures that could eventually displace conventional CMOS in certain high-performance computing applications — provided both development fees and a long-range technology roadmap alignment that few commercial foundry customers could replicate.

Programme-driven DoD revenue carried a different risk profile from commercial foundry revenue. Individual programme completions or budget-cycle delays produced quarter-to-quarter volatility that could obscure the underlying continuity of customer relationships. SkyWater managed this by maintaining a diversified programme slate across classification levels and customer agencies, reducing single-programme concentration without sacrificing the Trusted Foundry positioning that made DoD revenue defensible against offshore competition by structural, not merely economic, means.

The 2024–2026 period saw DoD electronics spending oriented toward electronic warfare, space and satellite payloads, and autonomous systems — application areas that drove demand for the RF SOI, mixed-signal CMOS, and specialty packaging capabilities at the core of SkyWater's process library. That alignment between US defence investment priorities and the company's specific capability profile provided demand visibility extending meaningfully into the 2027–2028 programme horizon.

## The 2026–2030 Horizon

The strategic posture SkyWater carried into 2026 rested on three interlocking execution requirements. First, ATS-to-Wafer conversion: the development programmes seeded in 2022–2024 needed to reach volume production without programme cancellation or customer schedule slippage that would defer revenue recognition. Second, Florida CoN ramp: Kissimmee needed to progress from qualification volumes to utilisation levels that contributed meaningfully to fixed-cost absorption and reduced the per-wafer overhead drag that had widened operating losses during the ramp. Third, ~~CHIPS Act deployment~~ ==federal capital deployment==: ~~federal capital~~ ==CHIPS dollars at Bloomington and EDA/DoD dollars at Florida== needed to be translated into productive capacity additions that compressed the timeline to operating leverage without creating the organisational strain of a build pace that outran qualified process engineers.

Against those requirements, the competitive environment offered both tailwind and friction. The broader US foundry-policy environment — CHIPS Act incentives, Export Administration Regulations tightening on China-bound semiconductor equipment, and the reshoring of defence electronics sourcing — provided structural demand support that was largely indifferent to cyclical semiconductor swings. Scaled competitors were also moving, however. TSMC's Arizona fabs, oriented toward leading-edge logic at 4nm and below, carry a brand gravity that attracts fabless design teams who might otherwise have explored specialty process alternatives at smaller foundries.

SkyWater's durable differentiator through this period remained the depth of its specialty process library and the Trusted Foundry relationship that made it the default choice for programmes requiring domestic-only production in process families — superconducting electronics, MEMS, RF SOI variants — that GlobalFoundries did not maintain at equivalent maturity. That specificity, combined with ~~CHIPS Act capital supporting capacity expansion~~ ==CHIPS Act capital supporting Bloomington capacity expansion and state/DoD-backed build-out in Florida==, and a Florida CoN adding a second ==active== manufacturing node, defined a company whose 2026–2030 trajectory depended less on conquering new market segments than on executing the programme pipeline it had already assembled — and on demonstrating, at last, that the eighteen-to-thirty-six-month conversion lag that had always been the thesis was now also becoming the revenue line.

## C. Glossary of Terms

**Advanced Technology Services (ATS):** Engineering-intensive process development contracts, typically government or development-stage commercial customers. Revenue recognized as milestones are achieved. Upstream to Wafer Services.

**Wafer Services:** Production-volume semiconductor manufacturing on processes previously developed under ATS. Recurring, scalable revenue with superior margin characteristics relative to ATS.

**DoD Trusted Foundry:** Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA) designation enabling SkyWater to produce classified and export-controlled semiconductor devices for US government programs. Sole-Source eligible.

**Center of Neovation (CoN):** Advanced packaging and emerging-technology facility in Kissimmee, Florida; leased from Osceola County under a public-private structure; ~~principal site for CHIPS Act-supported capacity expansion.~~ ==funded principally through Florida state EDA incentives and DoD program awards rather than a direct CHIPS Act grant.==

**CHIPS and Science Act (2022):** US federal legislation appropriating approximately $52 billion for domestic semiconductor manufacturing incentives and R&D. SkyWater a recipient ==of a CHIPS Program Office PMT== for Bloomington modernization ~~and Florida CoN expansion~~==; the Florida CoN is supported through separate Florida state EDA and DoD channels, not a direct CHIPS Act award==.

| X-Fab | Specialty analog/mixed-signal foundry; European-headquartered; no US Trusted Foundry status |
| Tower Semiconductor | Specialty analog and RF; Israeli-headquartered; Intel acquisition blocked 2023 |

SkyWater's competitive differentiation rests on the combination of US ownership, DoD Trusted Foundry certification, and specialty process breadth (RF SOI, MEMS, superconducting electronics, advanced packaging) unavailable in that configuration at any single peer.
